Bachelor’s Thesis
Principal Bundles and Gauge Theories

Matthijs Vákár Affiliation: Student number 3367428 Affiliation: Universiteit Utrecht
Utrecht, June 21, 2011

Supervisor: Erik van den Ban

Preface

Principal bundles are of great mathematical importance. It will be argued that, in some sense, they are the best fibre bundles for a given structure group, from which all others can be constructed. For instance, one can use one principal bundle to understand all tensor bundles of a vector bundle or one principal bundle to understand all (Dirac and non-Dirac) spinor bundles. Moreover, they encode the structure of certain nice (i.e. smooth, free, and proper) group actions on a manifold. It is clear that these objects could be studied in their own right, without any physical applications.

On the other hand, they are arguably the most important spaces in modern physics. They arise when we want to resolve the issue that we are trying to give an intrinsic description of nature, while all measurements made with respect to the reference frame of some observer are non-intrinsic – one might even argue that they say as much about the observer as about the observed. They are the spaces on which certain modern field theories describing elementary particle interactions, called gauge theories, are formulated, even if the physicists themselves are not very explicit about it.

Mathematicians often equip principal bundles with some extra geometrical structure called a principal connection. These are the natural generalisations of the affine connections we know from Riemannian geometry. They have been an object of study in pure mathematics ever since Cartan. Following the famous paper by Yang and Mills in 1954, a theory of elementary particle physics was built using precisely this kind of mathematics (without being aware of it). However, as is often the case in physics and mathematics, communication was rather sporadic and it was realised only later that the physicists had been studying precisely what the mathematicians had already worked out years before. [21]

It should be clear that the subject of principal bundles with connections, sometimes called gauge theory, is of interest from a mathematical perspective as well as from a physical one. This is also clear from the amount of material on the subject published in both disciplines. However, little has been written that would satisfy both mathematicians and physicists - as far as I am concerned, only [6] comes close to doing this. Although I have no illusions of filling this gap, I will try to give an introduction to the subject from both points of view. Although most results in this thesis are not original - probably with the exception of the category-theoretic ones, especially those in section 1.1 - I presume that the presentation and the derivations are less conventional.

I assume that the reader has some familiarity with manifold geometry and the classical field theories of general relativity and electromagnetism. Naturally, I first discuss the mathematics of the subject and only then proceed to the physical side of the story, of which I unfortunately cover only the tip of the iceberg, restricting myself to a brief introduction to non-second-quantised gauge theories of the Yang-Mills kind. I have tried to keep both accounts as separate as possible, although the chapter on physics rests heavily on the mathematical preliminaries. Almost all results that are proven in the chapter on mathematics have some application in physics, even if this application is not entirely clear from this thesis.

Key Insights

While writing this thesis, I have had a few insights that now form the guiding thread of the text. The reader might want to bear these in mind.

  1. 1.

    Mathematical insight: Principal bundles are bundles of frames of their associated bundles. We can formulate this principle as an equivalence of categories between principal GG-bundles and (G,λ)(G,\lambda)-fibre bundles for an effective action λ\lambda.

  2. 2.

    Mathematical insight: It should be possible to construct categories of (G,λ)(G,\lambda)-fibre bundles with appropriate connections. (In the case of G​L​(𝕜k)GL(\Bbbk^{k}) these would be affine connections.) Then the equivalence of item 1 should extend to an equivalence of categories between principal bundles with principal connections and these (G,λ)(G,\lambda)-bundles with (G,λ)(G,\lambda)-connections. In the case of G​L​(𝕜k)GL(\Bbbk^{k}) it is clear from this thesis that this is true and we should easily be able to prove the general claim in an analogous way.

  3. 3.

    Didactic insight: Using this equivalence, we can view principal bundles with principal connections (which arise in particle physics) as a generalisation of vector bundles with affine connections (which arise in general relativity), the generalising step being the replacement of G​L​(𝕜k)GL(\Bbbk^{k}) by an arbitrary Lie group GG.

  4. 4.

    Physical insight: Because of item 1, principal bundles are the natural context for many physical gauge theories. Principal connections naturally arise when we try to give a geometric description of gauge-invariant interactions. Principal bundles with connections may serve as a unifying language in physics. Not only do they provide a mathematically rigorous framework for first-quantised gauge field theories, but they also give geometric interpretations for the physicists’ calculations, helping to create an overview of this vast subject.

Notation and Conventions

Throughout the text, maps and actions will be assumed to be smooth, i.e. C∞C^{\infty}, unless stated otherwise.

At times, we use the notation m∈Mm\in M, g∈Gg\in G, s∈Ss\in S, f∈Ff\in F, p∈Pp\in P, v∈Vv\in V, without further comment. Moreover, principal connection 11-forms are denoted by ω\omega and equivariant maps in C∞​(P,W)C^{\infty}(P,W) from a principal GG-bundle to a vector space with a GG-action are denoted by ψ\psi.

If F⟶πMF\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\pi}}{{\longrightarrow}}M is a fibre bundle and m∈Mm\in M, FmF_{m} denotes the fibre of π\pi over mm: π−1​(m)\pi^{-1}(m). Moreover, we use the conventional abuse of notation, sometimes writing FF for a fibre bundle instead of F⟶πMF\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\pi}}{{\longrightarrow}}M. A second abuse of notation is the dot notation for a group action if there is no ambiguity in which action we mean.

A glossary of notation can be found at the end of this thesis.

Chapter 1 Fibre Bundles and Connections

1.1 Categories of Fibre Bundles

I know from personal experience that the notion of a fibre bundle can be a very confusing one, if it is not introduced properly. This is because there are many different but related variants, and their definitions include many subtleties. Moreover, it is very hard to find a good account of these in the literature. I will therefore begin this thesis with some very strict categorical definitions in this domain, most of which I have had to formulate myself, since I could not find them in the literature11 1 The book that comes closest is the classic reference [28] by Steenrod..

These definitions allow us to interpret the associated bundle construction as defining an equivalence of categories (for an effective action). This result sets the tone for this entire thesis. If one reads between the lines in many books, it seems that some form of this result must be known, although it has not been (as far as I know) stated explicitly. Starting from this abstract point of view, I will gradually specialise to more specific variants of fibre bundles.

Definition (Fibre bundle).

A fibre bundle with standard fibre SS is the combination of

  1. 1.

    a smooth22 2 Most of this theory can be developed in equal generality for the case of topological spaces, instead of smooth manifolds. However, from now on, we shall assume that we are working with the latter, since the smooth structure is essential to formulate the equations of many physical theories. manifold SS, called the fibre,

  2. 2.

    a map of manifolds F⟶πMF\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\pi}}{{\longrightarrow}}M, called the bundle projection from the total space FF onto the base space MM,

such that for each m∈Mm\in M, there exists a local trivialisation, i.e. a neighbourhood UU of mm in MM, such that π−1​(U)≅U×S\pi^{-1}(U)\cong U\times S via a fibre-respecting diffeomorphism:

We define a map of fibre bundles π⟶kπ′\pi\stackrel{{\scriptstyle k}}{{\longrightarrow}}\pi^{\prime} to be a tuple of maps F⟶kF′F\stackrel{{\scriptstyle k}}{{\longrightarrow}}F^{\prime} and M⟶kMM′M\stackrel{{\scriptstyle k_{M}}}{{\longrightarrow}}M^{\prime} such that

By a map of fibre bundles over MM, we mean a map π⟶kπ′\pi\stackrel{{\scriptstyle k}}{{\longrightarrow}}\pi^{\prime} between fibre bundles for which M=M′M=M^{\prime}. Note that for some authors kMk_{M} might still be nontrivial; here I mean the more restrictive case in which kM=idMk_{M}=\mathrm{id}_{M}.

This gives a category F​BFB of fibre bundles and a category F​BMFB_{M} of fibre bundles over MM, where composition is defined as one would expect.

One often has preferred local trivialisations (Uα,ψα)(U_{\alpha},\psi_{\alpha}) on a fibre bundle. A set of such local trivialisations such that (Uα)(U_{\alpha}) covers MM is called a fibre bundle atlas. Then, for each α,β\alpha,\beta there exists a unique function (Uα∩Uβ)×S⟶ϕα​βS(U_{\alpha}\cap U_{\beta})\times S\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\phi_{\alpha\beta}}}{{\longrightarrow}}S, such that ψα∘ψβ−1​(m,s)=(m,ϕα​β​(m,s))\psi_{\alpha}\circ\psi_{\beta}^{-1}(m,s)=(m,\phi_{\alpha\beta}(m,s)). Equivalently, we find transition functions Uα∩Uβ⟶ϕα​βDiff​SU_{\alpha}\cap U_{\beta}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\phi_{\alpha\beta}}}{{\longrightarrow}}\mathrm{Diff}\;S, with ϕα​β​(m)​(s)=ϕα​β​(m,s)\phi_{\alpha\beta}(m)(s)=\phi_{\alpha\beta}(m,s). Obviously, these maps (ϕα​β)(\phi_{\alpha\beta}) satisfy the Čech cocycle condition ϕα​β​(m)⋅ϕβ​γ​(m)=ϕα​γ​(m)\phi_{\alpha\beta}(m)\cdot\phi_{\beta\gamma}(m)=\phi_{\alpha\gamma}(m). A fibre bundle together with such a fibre bundle atlas is called a fibre bundle with coordinates or, briefly, a coordinate fibre bundle.

1.1.1 Coordinate (G,λ)(G,\lambda)-Bundles

Unfortunately, the group Diff​S\mathrm{Diff}\;S is difficult to handle. For instance, we run into trouble when we try to endow it with a smooth structure. It turns out to have a natural structure of an infinite-dimensional manifold (a Fréchet manifold if SS is compact), in which, indeed, the group operations are smooth maps. [22] This would lead to many technicalities. Fortunately, for many important examples of fibre bundles these transition functions only take values in a small part of Diff​S\mathrm{Diff}\;S. To be precise, often, we can find a Lie group GG, together with an action G×S⟶λSG\times S\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\lambda}}{{\longrightarrow}}S, such that the ϕα​β\phi_{\alpha\beta} factor through λ\lambda. That is, we can find maps Uα∩Uβ⟶gα​βGU_{\alpha}\cap U_{\beta}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle g_{\alpha\beta}}}{{\longrightarrow}}G, such that λ∘gα​β=ϕα​β\lambda\circ g_{\alpha\beta}=\phi_{\alpha\beta}:

The special case of an effective action λ\lambda, i.e. where we can interpret λ\lambda as an (algebraic) embedding G⟶λDiff​SG\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\lambda}}{{\longrightarrow}}\mathrm{Diff}\;S, will turn out to be of special importance since the fibre bundles corresponding to these actions can be characterised in a coordinate-free way (by a maximal atlas). This leads to the following definitions.

Definition (GG-cocycle).

Let MM be a manifold and GG a Lie group. We define a GG-cocycle of transition functions on it to be the combination of

  1. 1.

    an open cover (Uα)(U_{\alpha}),

  2. 2.

    a family of smooth mappings Uα∩Uβ⟶gα​βGU_{\alpha}\cap U_{\beta}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle g_{\alpha\beta}}}{{\longrightarrow}}G, which satisfies the cocycle condition gα​β​(m)⋅gβ​γ​(m)=gα​γ​(m)g_{\alpha\beta}(m)\cdot g_{\beta\gamma}(m)=g_{\alpha\gamma}(m), for all m∈Uα∩Uβ∩Uγm\in U_{\alpha}\cap U_{\beta}\cap U_{\gamma} and gα​α​(m)=eg_{\alpha\alpha}(m)=e.

We understand a map of cocycles to consist of

  1. 1.

    a map M⟶hM′M\stackrel{{\scriptstyle h}}{{\longrightarrow}}M^{\prime},

  2. 2.

    a tuple of cocycles (Uα,gα​β)(U_{\alpha},g_{\alpha\beta}) on MM and (Uα′,gα​β′)(U^{\prime}_{\alpha},g^{\prime}_{\alpha\beta}) on M′M^{\prime},

  3. 3.

    maps Uβ∩h−1​(Uα′)⟶hα​βGU_{\beta}\cap h^{-1}(U^{\prime}_{\alpha})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle h_{\alpha\beta}}}{{\longrightarrow}}G,

such that hα​β​(m)⋅gβ​γ​(m)=hα​γ​(m)h_{\alpha\beta}(m)\cdot g_{\beta\gamma}(m)=h_{\alpha\gamma}(m), for m∈Uγ∩Uβ∩h−1​(Uα′)m\in U_{\gamma}\cap U_{\beta}\cap h^{-1}(U^{\prime}_{\alpha}) and gα​β′​(h⁡(m))⋅hβ​γ​(m)=hα​γ​(m)g^{\prime}_{\alpha\beta}(h(m))\cdot h_{\beta\gamma}(m)=h_{\alpha\gamma}(m), for m∈Uγ∩h−1​(Uβ′∩Uα′)m\in U_{\gamma}\cap h^{-1}(U^{\prime}_{\beta}\cap U^{\prime}_{\alpha}).

It is easily seen that the GG-cocycles on smooth manifolds form a category C​CGCC^{G}, where the composition of (h,(Uα,gα​β),(Uα′,gα​β′),hα​β)(h,(U_{\alpha},g_{\alpha\beta}),(U^{\prime}_{\alpha},g^{\prime}_{\alpha\beta}),h_{\alpha\beta}) and (i,(Uα′,gα​β′),(Uα′′,gα​β′′),iα​β)(i,(U^{\prime}_{\alpha},g^{\prime}_{\alpha\beta}),(U^{\prime\prime}_{\alpha},g^{\prime\prime}_{\alpha\beta}),i_{\alpha\beta}) is defined to be (i∘h,(Uα,gα​β),(Uα′′,gα​β′′),(i∘h)α​β)(i\circ h,(U_{\alpha},g_{\alpha\beta}),(U^{\prime\prime}_{\alpha},g^{\prime\prime}_{\alpha\beta}),(i\circ h)_{\alpha\beta}), with (i∘h)α​γ​(m):=iα​β​(h⁡(m))⋅hβ​γ​(m)(i\circ h)_{\alpha\gamma}(m):=i_{\alpha\beta}(h(m))\cdot h_{\beta\gamma}(m)33 3 This is immediately seen to be independent of the choice of β\beta..

Definition (Coordinate (G,λ)(G,\lambda)-bundle structure).

Suppose F⟶πMF\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\pi}}{{\longrightarrow}}M is a fibre bundle, with standard fibre SS, GG a Lie group and G×S⟶λSG\times S\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\lambda}}{{\longrightarrow}}S is a left action of GG on SS. A (G,λ)(G,\lambda)-fibre bundle with coordinates or, briefly, a coordinate (G,λ)(G,\lambda)-bundle structure on π\pi for the action λ\lambda consists of

  1. 1.

    a GG-cocycle (Uα,gα​β)(U_{\alpha},g_{\alpha\beta}) on MM,

  2. 2.

    a fibre bundle atlas (Uα,ψα)(U_{\alpha},\psi_{\alpha}),

such that ψα∘ψβ−1​(m,s)=(m,λ⁡(gα​β​(m),s))\psi_{\alpha}\circ\psi_{\beta}^{-1}(m,s)=(m,\lambda(g_{\alpha\beta}(m),s)). A coordinate (G,λ)(G,\lambda)-bundle is also called a coordinate GG-bundle if there is no ambiguity about the action λ\lambda.

We understand a map of coordinate GG-bundles to consist of

  1. 1.

    a map of cocycles (h,(Uα,gα​β),(Uα′,gα​β′),hα​β)(h,(U_{\alpha},g_{\alpha\beta}),(U^{\prime}_{\alpha},g^{\prime}_{\alpha\beta}),h_{\alpha\beta}),

  2. 2.

    a map of fibre bundles:

such that kM=hk_{M}=h and ψα′∘k∘ψβ−1​(m,s)=(kM​(m),λ⁡(hα​β​(m),s))\psi^{\prime}_{\alpha}\circ k\circ\psi_{\beta}^{-1}(m,s)=(k_{M}(m),\lambda(h_{\alpha\beta}(m),s)).

Again, we can form a category, which we shall call C​F​BλCFB^{\lambda}, where the composition is understood to be the simultaneous composition of maps of cocycles and of fibre bundles.

Note that, in both categories C​CGCC^{G} and C​F​BλCFB^{\lambda}, the isomorphisms are precisely those maps that are diffeomorphisms on the base space.

One can wonder if it is possible to construct a fibre bundle from an arbitrary (G,λ)(G,\lambda)-cocycle. The (affirmative) answer is given by the well-known fibre bundle construction theorem. Here, I formulate a categorical version of this theorem.

Theorem 1.1.1 (Fibre bundle construction theorem).

Let G×S⟶λSG\times S\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\lambda}}{{\longrightarrow}}S be a smooth group action. We then have an equivalence of categories

CCG⇆C​UλC​BλCFBλ.CC^{G}\mathop{\leftrightarrows}^{CU^{\lambda}}_{CB^{\lambda}}CFB^{\lambda}.
Proof.

We define the functor C​UλCU^{\lambda} as the obvious forgetful functor that sends a coordinate (G,λ)(G,\lambda)-bundle (π,Uα,ψα,gα​β)(\pi,U_{\alpha},\psi_{\alpha},g_{\alpha\beta}) to the cocycle (Uα,gα​β)(U_{\alpha},g_{\alpha\beta}) and a map of coordinate bundles to its map of cocycles. Functoriality holds by definition44 4 Moreover, I defined the composition of maps of cocycles in this way, so that functoriality would hold. of the composition in C​F​BλCFB^{\lambda}.

The definition of the functor C​BλCB^{\lambda} is the non-trivial part of the equivalence. We proceed by first defining it on objects. Suppose we are given a cocycle (Uα,gα​β)∈C​CG(U_{\alpha},g_{\alpha\beta})\in CC^{G} on MM. Write Σ\Sigma for the topological coproduct ⨆αUα×S\bigsqcup_{\alpha}U_{\alpha}\times S. To be explicit, we understand the underlying set to be ⋃α{α}×Uα×S\bigcup_{\alpha}\{\alpha\}\times U_{\alpha}\times S. On this topological space, we define an equivalence relation:

{α}×Uα×S∋(α,m,s)∼(β,m′,s′)∈{β}×Uβ×Siff(m,s)=(m′,gα​β​(m)⋅s′).\{\alpha\}\times U_{\alpha}\times S\ni(\alpha,m,s)\sim(\beta,m^{\prime},s^{\prime})\in\{\beta\}\times U_{\beta}\times S\quad\textnormal{iff}\quad(m,s)=(m^{\prime},g_{\alpha\beta}(m)\cdot s^{\prime}).

Note that the fact that this is an equivalence relation follows directly from the cocycle condition. We can divide out this relation and give F:=Σ/∼F:=\Sigma/\sim the quotient topology. Note that there exists a natural projection Σ⟶π′M\Sigma\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\pi^{\prime}}}{{\longrightarrow}}M, which we obtain by the fact that we have a projection Uα×S⟶π1Uα⟶iαMU_{\alpha}\times S\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\pi_{1}}}{{\longrightarrow}}U_{\alpha}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle i_{\alpha}}}{{\longrightarrow}}M, where π1\pi_{1} is the projection onto UαU_{\alpha} and iαi_{\alpha} is the obvious inclusion, for each term in the coproduct. Since points that are related by ∼\sim project along π′\pi^{\prime} to the same element, this projection descends to the quotient: F⟶πMF\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\pi}}{{\longrightarrow}}M.

The trivialisations (ψα)(\psi_{\alpha}) of the bundle are then defined as one would expect: ψα​([α,m,s]):=(m,s)\psi_{\alpha}([\alpha,m,s]):=(m,s), if we write [α,m,s]∈F[\alpha,m,s]\in F for the equivalence class of (α,m,s)∈Σ(\alpha,m,s)\in\Sigma. This map is well-defined since (α,m,s)∼(α,m′,s′)(\alpha,m,s)\sim(\alpha,m^{\prime},s^{\prime}) iff (m,s)=(m′,s′)(m,s)=(m^{\prime},s^{\prime}). It is a homeomorphism since it is an inverse to the restriction of the quotient map.

To see that FF is a Hausdorff space, suppose that f,f′∈Ff,f^{\prime}\in F are two distinct points. If π⁡(f)≠π⁡(f′)\pi(f)\neq\pi(f^{\prime}), we can separate them in MM, which is Hausdorff, and take the inverse image under π\pi to obtain distinct neighbourhoods in FF. Otherwise, we can separate ff and f′f^{\prime} in one chart ψα\psi_{\alpha}, since we know SS to be Hausdorff. To see that FF is second countable, note that MM is so. Therefore, we can find a countable refinement (Ui′)(U^{\prime}_{i}) of (Uα)(U_{\alpha}). Then, each Ui′U^{\prime}_{i} lies in the domain of a local trivialisation ψαi\psi_{\alpha_{i}}. Since SS is second countable, we find a countable basis (Vj)(V_{j}) for its topology. We conclude that ∪i,j(ψαi−1(Ui′×Vj))\cup_{i,j}(\psi_{\alpha_{i}}^{-1}(U^{\prime}_{i}\times V_{j})) is a basis for the topology of FF. It is clearly countable.

We conclude that we have constructed a topological fibre bundle F⟶πMF\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\pi}}{{\longrightarrow}}M. We want to show that π\pi has structure group (G,λ)(G,\lambda). For this, suppose that Uα∩Uβ≠∅U_{\alpha}\cap U_{\beta}\neq\emptyset. Then, m∈Uα∩Uβm\in U_{\alpha}\cap U_{\beta} implies that ψβ−1​(m,s)∈π−1​(Uα∩Uβ)=π−1​(Uα)∩π−1​(Uβ)\psi_{\beta}^{-1}(m,s)\in\pi^{-1}(U_{\alpha}\cap U_{\beta})=\pi^{-1}(U_{\alpha})\cap\pi^{-1}(U_{\beta}). Since ψβ−1​(m,s)∈π−1​(Uα)\psi_{\beta}^{-1}(m,s)\in\pi^{-1}(U_{\alpha}), we can write it as [α,m′,s′][\alpha,m^{\prime},s^{\prime}] for some m′∈Uα,s′∈Sm^{\prime}\in U_{\alpha},\;s^{\prime}\in S. Then, however, m=m′m=m^{\prime} and s′=gα​β​(m)⋅ss^{\prime}=g_{\alpha\beta}(m)\cdot s, by definition of ∼\sim. We conclude that ψβ−1​(m,s)=[α,m,gα​β​(m)⋅s]\psi_{\beta}^{-1}(m,s)=[\alpha,m,g_{\alpha\beta}(m)\cdot s] and therefore ψα∘ψβ−1​(m,s)=(m,gα​β​(m)⋅s)\psi_{\alpha}\circ\psi_{\beta}^{-1}(m,s)=(m,g_{\alpha\beta}(m)\cdot s). Now, the smooth structure on FF is obtained from that on SS by the maps (ψα)(\psi_{\alpha}). This gives a consistent notion of smoothness precisely because the transition functions act by the (smooth) action of a Lie group. This is a remarkable result. It means that any two categories C​F​BλCFB^{\lambda} and C​F​BμCFB^{\mu} are equivalent for any two GG-actions μ\mu and λ\lambda on a manifold. We may even be dealing with a situation in which μ\mu and λ\lambda are actions on two different manifolds. In this sense, the cocycle structure actually encodes precisely all relevant information about the coordinate GG-bundle.

For each Lie group GG, there is one particularly easy canonical choice for a smooth GG-action, namely the action LL of GG on itself by left multiplication. We can take the category C​F​BLCFB^{L} as a representative of the equivalence class of categories equivalent to C​CGCC^{G}. The objects of this category are known as coordinate principal GG-bundles. (This may explain the name.) Therefore we also write C​P​BGCPB^{G} for C​F​BLCFB^{L}.

1.1.2 (G,λ)(G,\lambda)-Bundles

Since, in modern differential geometry, we would like our theory to be coordinate-independent, we say that some coordinate (G,λ)(G,\lambda)-bundle structures are equivalent and describe the same (G,λ)(G,\lambda)-fibre bundle. Compare this with manifold theory, where a differentiable manifold is defined as a topological space, together with an equivalence class of coordinate atlases. Similarly, we can also define an equivalence relation on the coordinate (G,λ)(G,\lambda)-bundle structures for a given G×S⟶λSG\times S\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\lambda}}{{\longrightarrow}}S. We say that two coordinate (G,λ)(G,\lambda)-bundle structures (Uα,ψα,gα​β)(U_{\alpha},\psi_{\alpha},g_{\alpha\beta}) and (U~α,ψ~α,g~α​β)(\tilde{U}_{\alpha},\tilde{\psi}_{\alpha},\tilde{g}_{\alpha\beta}) for the fibre bundle F⟶πMF\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\pi}}{{\longrightarrow}}M are strictly equivalent (in the terminology of [28]) if there exist smooth maps Uβ∩U~α⟶tα​βGU_{\beta}\cap\tilde{U}_{\alpha}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle t_{\alpha\beta}}}{{\longrightarrow}}G, such that ψ~α∘ψβ−1​(m,s)=(m,tα​β​(m)⋅s)\tilde{\psi}_{\alpha}\circ\psi_{\beta}^{-1}(m,s)=(m,t_{\alpha\beta}(m)\cdot s), for all s∈Ss\in S. Such an equivalence class is called a (G,λ)(G,\lambda)-fibre bundle. One can compare these with the equivalence classes of atlases that correspond to manifold structures on a topological space. Again, one more often speaks simply of GG-bundles and considers the action λ\lambda to be understood.

These objects are spaces that are ubiquitous in theoretical physics. They are of special importance in studying classical field theories. Therefore, it is useful to define a category F​BλFB^{\lambda} which has these (G,λ)(G,\lambda)-fibre bundles as objects. A natural definition for the arrows of this category is that they are equivalence classes of arrows in C​F​BλCFB^{\lambda} corresponding to the same map F⟶kF′F\stackrel{{\scriptstyle k}}{{\longrightarrow}}F^{\prime} of fibre bundles. Of course, again, the isomorphisms in F​BλFB^{\lambda} are precisely those maps that are diffeomorphisms on the base space. Note that this gives us an obvious quotient functor C​F​Bλ⟶QλF​BλCFB^{\lambda}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle Q^{\lambda}}}{{\longrightarrow}}FB^{\lambda} which ‘forgets’ the particular cocycle structure, i.e. it sends each object and arrow to its equivalence class in the sense described above. Note also that we have the obvious functorial embedding F​Bλ⟶F​BFB^{\lambda}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle}}{{\longrightarrow}}FB. Of course, this also gives us a category P​BG:=F​BLPB^{G}:=FB^{L} of principal GG-bundles.

1.1.3 Principal Bundles

Note that, since we also have a right GG-action RR on GG that commutes with LL, we can define a global right GG-action ρ\rho on PP, if P⟶π~MP\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\tilde{\pi}}}{{\longrightarrow}}M is a principal GG-bundle. This is the action that looks like right multiplication in a local trivialisation. Obviously, this action, called the principal right action restricts to a transitive, free action on each fibre. Therefore, GG acts freely on PP. Moreover, this action on PP is easily seen to be proper. These properties turn out precisely to characterise the fact that a fibre bundle P⟶π~MP\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\tilde{\pi}}}{{\longrightarrow}}M is a principal GG-bundle. [4]

Theorem 1.1.2 (Quotient manifold theorem).

Let ρ\rho be a right action of a Lie group GG on a manifold PP. Then the following conditions are equivalent:

  1. 1.

    The action is proper and free.

  2. 2.

    The quotient map P⟶π~P/GP\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\tilde{\pi}}}{{\longrightarrow}}P/G is a principal fibre bundle55 5 In particular, since the action is proper and free, the quotient space P/GP/G has a unique smooth structure such that the quotient map P⟶π~P/GP\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\tilde{\pi}}}{{\longrightarrow}}P/G is a smooth submersion. with ρ\rho as a principal right action.

It is easier to see what maps of principal bundles are. Of course, they are a special kind of maps of fibre bundles between principal bundles. The property that precisely captures the fact that they are maps of principal bundles is that they intertwine both principal right actions.66 6 It should be noted that, although this is a common definition of a map of principal bundles and it is used in, for example, the standard reference on fibre bundles, [15], the standard reference on principal bundles, [18], uses a broader class of maps. They define a map of principal bundles to be the combination of a map π~⟶kπ~′\tilde{\pi}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle k}}{{\longrightarrow}}\tilde{\pi}^{\prime} of fibre bundles from the principal GG-bundle π~\tilde{\pi} to the principal G′G^{\prime}-bundle π~′\tilde{\pi}^{\prime} and a homomorphism G⟶fG′G\stackrel{{\scriptstyle f}}{{\longrightarrow}}G^{\prime} of groups, such that k∘ρg=ρf⁡(g)′∘kk\circ\rho_{g}=\rho^{\prime}_{f(g)}\circ k, for all g∈Gg\in G. (Here ρ\rho and ρ′\rho^{\prime} denote both principal right actions.) Let us denote the category of all principal fibre bundles with this larger collection of maps by P​BPB. This category has some advantages as it can be used to describe more phenomena, like maps between principal bundles with different structure groups. As a consequence, the restriction of P​BPB to some fixed base space MM on which the arrows are demanded to be the identity, P​BMPB_{M} has finite products. Indeed, these products arise in Yang-Mills theories. At this point, however, I see no possibility to adjust the definition of a map of (G,λ)(G,\lambda)-bundles to fit this definition. For instance, I cannot see how the associated bundle functor, which can be defined for a G′G^{\prime}-action λ\lambda and a map (P,G)⟶(k,f)(P′,G′)(P,G)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle(k,f)}}{{\longrightarrow}}(P^{\prime},G^{\prime}) to be the obvious map P⁡[λ∘f]⟶k⁡[λ]P′​[λ]P[\lambda\circ f]\stackrel{{\scriptstyle k[\lambda]}}{{\longrightarrow}}P^{\prime}[\lambda], would extend to an equivalence from this category. To see this, note that for a map of principal GG-bundles

the following holds if we choose corresponding principal GG-bundle atlases (Uα,ψα,gα​β)(U_{\alpha},\psi_{\alpha},g_{\alpha\beta}) and (Uα′,ψα′,gα​β′)(U^{\prime}_{\alpha},\psi^{\prime}_{\alpha},g^{\prime}_{\alpha\beta}):

ψα′​(k⁡(ρ⁡(ψβ−1​(m,g1),g2)))\displaystyle\psi_{\alpha}^{\prime}(k(\rho(\psi_{\beta}^{-1}(m,g_{1}),g_{2}))) =ψα′∘k∘ψβ−1​(m,g1⋅g2)\displaystyle=\psi_{\alpha}^{\prime}\circ k\circ\psi_{\beta}^{-1}(m,g_{1}\cdot g_{2})
=(kM​(m),hα​β​(m)⋅(g1⋅g2))\displaystyle=(k_{M}(m),h_{\alpha\beta}(m)\cdot(g_{1}\cdot g_{2}))
=(kM​(m),(hα​β​(m)⋅g1)⋅g2)\displaystyle=(k_{M}(m),(h_{\alpha\beta}(m)\cdot g_{1})\cdot g_{2})
=ψα′​(ρ⁡(ψα′−1​(ψα′​(k⁡(ψβ−1​(m,g1)))),g2))\displaystyle=\psi_{\alpha}^{\prime}(\rho(\psi_{\alpha}^{\prime-1}(\psi_{\alpha}^{\prime}(k(\psi_{\beta}^{-1}(m,g_{1})))),g_{2}))
=ψα′​(ρ⁡(k⁡(ψβ−1​(m,g1)),g2)),\displaystyle=\psi_{\alpha}^{\prime}(\rho(k(\psi_{\beta}^{-1}(m,g_{1})),g_{2})),

so kk intertwines the principal right actions (which I both denoted by ρ\rho). For the converse statement, note that the above also tells us how we should define hα​βh_{\alpha\beta} in terms of kk. It is easily checked that hα​βh_{\alpha\beta} is a map of cocycles if kk intertwines the actions.

1.1.4 A Coordinate-Free Equivalence

Note that, in the case of an effective action G×S⟶λSG\times S\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\lambda}}{{\longrightarrow}}S, the strict equivalence of (G,λ)(G,\lambda)-bundle structures can also be formulated as the statement that their union is again a (G,λ)(G,\lambda)-bundle structure with respect to the GG-valued transition functions which are uniquely determined since GG acts effectively. Therefore we can associate its maximal element to each equivalence class (given by the total union). We can also lift a map of (G,λ)(G,\lambda)-fibre bundles in a canonical way to a map between the maximal representatives of the equivalence classes. Indeed, define (m,hα​β​(m)⋅s):=ψ~α∘k∘ψβ−1​(m,s)(m,h_{\alpha\beta}(m)\cdot s):=\tilde{\psi}_{\alpha}\circ k\circ\psi_{\beta}^{-1}(m,s), if kk is the given fibre bundle map and (Uα,ψα)(U_{\alpha},\psi_{\alpha}) and (U~α,ψ~α)(\tilde{U}_{\alpha},\tilde{\psi}_{\alpha}) are the trivialisations of the maximal atlases on both GG-bundles. (Note that this defines hα​βh_{\alpha\beta} uniquely, since λ\lambda is effective.) Therefore, we obtain a canonical section F​Bλ⟶ΣλC​F​BλFB^{\lambda}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\Sigma^{\lambda}}}{{\longrightarrow}}CFB^{\lambda} of the quotient functor QλQ^{\lambda}. This will lead to a natural coordinate-free treatment of (G,λ)(G,\lambda)-fibre bundles when λ\lambda is effective.

In light of this discussion on a coordinate-free notion of a (G,λ)(G,\lambda)-fibre bundle, it is natural to wonder if we can find an atlas-independent form of theorem 1.1.1. We can hope to succeed since the construction of Σλ\Sigma^{\lambda} is canonical. It turns out that we are at least able to obtain such a form for the equivalence between C​F​BλCFB^{\lambda} and C​F​BμCFB^{\mu} for λ,μ\lambda,\mu effective GG-actions. That is, we have the following.

Theorem 1.1.3.

Let G×S⟶λSG\times S\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\lambda}}{{\longrightarrow}}S and G×S′⟶μS′G\times S^{\prime}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mu}}{{\longrightarrow}}S^{\prime} be effective actions, i.e. λ,μ\lambda,\mu define (algebraic) embeddings of groups G↪Diff​S,Diff​S′G\hookrightarrow\mathrm{Diff}\;S,\;\mathrm{Diff}\;S^{\prime}. We then have an equivalence of categories

FBμ⇆Cλ​μCμ​λFBλ.FB^{\mu}\mathop{\leftrightarrows}^{C^{\lambda\mu}}_{C^{\mu\lambda}}FB^{\lambda}.
Proof.

The idea of the proof will be to use the functors of theorem 1.1.1 to construct the equivalence:

Put differently, it gives a coordinate-independent characterisation of GG-bundles. To realise this, we use the canonical sections Σλ\Sigma^{\lambda} and Σμ\Sigma^{\mu} for QλQ^{\lambda} and QμQ^{\mu} respectively, to construct the functors Cλ​μC^{\lambda\mu} and Cμ​λC^{\mu\lambda} exactly as one would expect. (Σλ∘Qλ\Sigma^{\lambda}\circ Q^{\lambda} extends the atlas to the maximal compatible one. The resulting coordinate (G,λ)(G,\lambda)-fibre bundle is by definition strictly equivalent to the one we started with.)

The proof will rest on the following observation: C​Uλ∘Σλ∘Qλ∘C​Bλ≅idC​CGCU^{\lambda}\circ\Sigma^{\lambda}\circ Q^{\lambda}\circ CB^{\lambda}\cong\mathrm{id}_{CC^{G}}. Therefore, we first verify this. Let 𝒞:=(Uα,gα​β)\mathcal{C}:=(U_{\alpha},g_{\alpha\beta}) be a GG-cocycle on MM. Then C​Bλ​(Uα,gα​β)=(π,Uα,ψα,gα​β)CB^{\lambda}(U_{\alpha},g_{\alpha\beta})=(\pi,U_{\alpha},\psi_{\alpha},g_{\alpha\beta}) is the corresponding coordinate (G,λ)(G,\lambda)-bundle. Now, Σλ∘Qλ∘C​Bλ​(Uα,gα​β)=(π,U~α,ψ~α,g~α​β)\Sigma^{\lambda}\circ Q^{\lambda}\circ CB^{\lambda}(U_{\alpha},g_{\alpha\beta})=(\pi,\tilde{U}_{\alpha},\tilde{\psi}_{\alpha},\tilde{g}_{\alpha\beta}) is the compatible maximal coordinate (G,λ)(G,\lambda)-bundle. Therefore, there exist smooth maps Uβ∩U~α⟶tα​βGU_{\beta}\cap\tilde{U}_{\alpha}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle t_{\alpha\beta}}}{{\longrightarrow}}G, such that ψ~α∘ψβ−1​(m,s)=(m,tα​β​(m)⋅s)\tilde{\psi}_{\alpha}\circ\psi_{\beta}^{-1}(m,s)=(m,t_{\alpha\beta}(m)\cdot s), for all s∈Ss\in S. Now, this allows us to define a map of GG-cocycles ϵ𝒞:=(idM,tα​β)\epsilon_{\mathcal{C}}:=(\mathrm{id}_{M},t_{\alpha\beta}) from 𝒞=(Uα,gα​β)\mathcal{C}=(U_{\alpha},g_{\alpha\beta}) to 𝒞~:=C​Uλ∘Σλ∘Qλ∘C​Bλ​(𝒞)=(U~α,g~α​β)\tilde{\mathcal{C}}:=CU^{\lambda}\circ\Sigma^{\lambda}\circ Q^{\lambda}\circ CB^{\lambda}(\mathcal{C})=(\tilde{U}_{\alpha},\tilde{g}_{\alpha\beta}). It is easily verified that this is indeed a map of cocycles. Indeed,

(m,tα​β​(m)⋅gβ​γ​(m)⋅s)\displaystyle(m,t_{\alpha\beta}(m)\cdot g_{\beta\gamma}(m)\cdot s) =ψ~α∘ψβ−1∘ψβ∘ψγ−1​(m,s)\displaystyle=\tilde{\psi}_{\alpha}\circ\psi_{\beta}^{-1}\circ\psi_{\beta}\circ\psi_{\gamma}^{-1}(m,s)
=ψ~α∘ψγ−1​(m,s)\displaystyle=\tilde{\psi}_{\alpha}\circ\psi_{\gamma}^{-1}(m,s)

Remark 1.1.4.

Perhaps the reader was expecting a direct analogue of theorem 1.1.1 in the form of an equivalence of categories between F​BλFB^{\lambda} and a category CGC^{G} that is obtained from C​CGCC^{G} by dividing out an equivalence relation on the objects and arrows. Indeed, I initially expected that such an equivalence would be an easy stepping stone to obtain the final result of theorem 1.1.1, which I really was trying to work towards. My candidate for the category CGC^{G} was one of cohomology classes of GG-cocycles as objects and some corresponding equivalence classes of arrows. This seemed the natural thing to do. Indeed, since my initial attempt I have found a result in [15] that establishes that there exists a (not necessarily natural) bijective correspondence between isomorphism classes of (G,λ)(G,\lambda)-fibre bundles and cohomology classes of GG-cocycles. However, my attempt failed because of the difficulty of constructing a canonical section of the quotient functor that sends a cocycle to its cohomology class. To obtain the categorical analogue of the result in Husemöller, one would like to have such a section to obtain one of the natural isomorphisms in the suspected equivalence of categories between F​BλFB^{\lambda} and CGC^{G}. However, it seems plausible that the result can still be proven without such a canonical section. One would then have to pick an arbitrary representative of every cohomology class and show that the final result does not depend on the choice that was made.

1.1.5 Associated Bundles and Generalised Frame Bundles

We have seen that, given a GG-cocycle on MM, there is one preferred GG-bundle that we can always construct: the principal GG-bundle. Therefore, given a (G,λ)(G,\lambda)-fibre bundle, we can construct the corresponding principal bundle from it, using theorem 1.1.3. The question arises what the relation is between our original fibre bundle and the principal bundle we constructed from it.

The answer is that the principal bundle can be given the interpretation of a bundle of generalised frames for the original fibre bundle or, reasoning in the other direction, that the fibre bundle is simply an associated bundle to the principal bundle. Both constructions can be understood to be functors. If we write LL for the action of GG on itself by left multiplication and let λ\lambda be an effective left GG action on SS, the generalised frame bundle functor FλF^{\lambda} is easily seen to be (naturally isomorphic to) Cλ​LC^{\lambda L}, while we will see that the associated bundle functor −[λ]-[\lambda] corresponds to CL​λC^{L\lambda}. Theorem 1.1.3 states that these two functors are each other’s pseudoinverse. I will discuss the explicit realisation of both constructions, starting with that of the so-called associated bundles.

Suppose we are given a principal bundle P⟶π~MP\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\tilde{\pi}}}{{\longrightarrow}}M with structure group GG. Then, for each (not necessarily effective) left action G×S⟶λSG\times S\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\lambda}}{{\longrightarrow}}S on a manifold SS, we can construct a right action P×S×G⟶RP×SP\times S\times G\stackrel{{\scriptstyle R}}{{\longrightarrow}}P\times S by (p,s,g)↦(p⋅g,g−1⋅s)(p,s,g)\mapsto(p\cdot g,g^{-1}\cdot s). This action is obviously free, since the principal action is. Properness can also easily be verified; however, this is somewhat technical, and we will therefore not write it out. Moreover, the action respects the fibre, and hence the quotient manifold theorem tells us that we can construct a so-called associated fibre bundle P×S/R=:P⁡[λ]⟶πMP\times S/R=:P[\lambda]\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\pi}}{{\longrightarrow}}M. (Here, π\pi is induced by the GG-invariant map P×S⟶π~∘π1MP\times S\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\tilde{\pi}\circ\pi_{1}}}{{\longrightarrow}}M.) However, following [19], we can also obtain the smooth structure on P⁡[λ]P[\lambda] in a different way, which ties in directly with the rest of our discussion.

In the case of an effective action λ\lambda, the associated bundle construction can equivalently be described as −[λ]≅CL​λ-[\lambda]\cong C^{L\lambda}.

Proof.

Therefore, there is also a general (pseudo)inverse construction to that of the associated bundle corresponding to an effective action. Indeed, suppose we are given a fibre bundle F⟶πMF\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\pi}}{{\longrightarrow}}M, with fibre SS and structure group GG that acts by an action λ\lambda. Then, as a consequence of theorem 1.1.3, Cλ​LC^{\lambda L} is a pseudoinverse to CL​λC^{L\lambda} and therefore also to −[λ]-[\lambda].

In particular, sections of Fλ​(F)F^{\lambda}(F) correspond to trivialisations of FF. if F⟶kF′F\stackrel{{\scriptstyle k}}{{\longrightarrow}}F^{\prime} is a map of (G,λ)(G,\lambda)-fibre bundles. We have obtained the following result.

Corollary 1.1.7.

We have a natural isomorphism Cλ​L≅FλC^{\lambda L}\cong F^{\lambda}, where FλF^{\lambda} is defined as described above.

Summarising, we have made the equivalence of categories

(which we had established for an effective action G×S⟶λSG\times S\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\lambda}}{{\longrightarrow}}S) concrete in the form of the associated bundle construction −[λ]≅CL​λ-[\lambda]\cong C^{L\lambda} and that of the generalised frame bundle Fλ≅Cλ​LF^{\lambda}\cong C^{\lambda L}. Naturally, these constructions are also each other’s pseudoinverse:

Therefore, whenever we encounter a (G,λ)(G,\lambda)-fibre bundle over a manifold MM, we can interpret it as an associated bundle of some principal GG-bundle over MM, which then takes on the role of a bundle of generalised frames for the original fibre bundle. This interpretation is of importance when trying to understand why principal bundles arise in physics.

Remark 1.1.8.

The reader might wonder why we have to demand that λ\lambda be effective to obtain the result that the associated bundle functor defines an equivalence of categories between P​BGPB^{G} and F​BλFB^{\lambda}. Indeed, we have seen that the associated bundle functor can be defined for arbitrary GG-actions. To see what can go wrong, consider the following (somewhat extreme) example. Let G×S⟶λSG\times S\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\lambda}}{{\longrightarrow}}S be the trivial action of a non-trivial Lie group GG on a one-point manifold S={p}S=\{p\}. Then we can construct a category F​Bλ≅MfdFB^{\lambda}\cong\mathrm{Mfd}, which is, of course, just isomorphic to the category of smooth manifolds. Moreover, we have an associated bundle functor P​BG⟶−[λ]F​Bλ≅MfdPB^{G}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle-[\lambda]}}{{\longrightarrow}}FB^{\lambda}\cong\mathrm{Mfd}, which just sends each principal bundle to its base space. Obviously, this functor is not faithful99 9 As is easily checked, it is full and essentially surjective on objects, though., so it cannot possibly define an equivalence of categories.

1.1.6 Vector Bundles and Principal G​L​(𝕜k)GL(\Bbbk^{k})-Bundles

An important special case of this equivalence of categories is that of the standard action λ\lambda of G​L​(𝕜k)GL(\Bbbk^{k}) on the vector space 𝕜k\Bbbk^{k}, where either 𝕜=ℝ\Bbbk=\mathbb{R} or 𝕜=ℂ\Bbbk=\mathbb{C}\;. Note that the objects of F​BλFB^{\lambda} are then just the kk-vector bundles over the field 𝕜\Bbbk, while the arrows are morphisms of vector bundles (morphisms of fibre bundles that are linear on the fibre) that are invertible on each fibre. We therefore also denote this category by V​B𝕜kVB^{k}_{\Bbbk}.

Let V⟶πMV\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\pi}}{{\longrightarrow}}M be a kk-vector bundle. The corresponding G​L​(𝕜k)GL(\Bbbk^{k})-principal bundle of linear frames Fλ​(V)⟶π~MF^{\lambda}(V)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\tilde{\pi}}}{{\longrightarrow}}M is often simply called the frame bundle. This can be regarded as the open subbundle of the Hom\mathrm{Hom}-bundle Hom⁡(𝕜k×M,V)\mathrm{Hom}(\Bbbk^{k}\times M,V) defined by the condition that the determinant is non-zero. Observe that the existence of a canonical basis for 𝕜k\Bbbk^{k} tells us that a (local) frame for a kk-vector bundle is the same as a set of kk linearly independent (local) sections of the bundle. The inverse construction P​BG​L​(𝕜k)⟶−[λ]V​B𝕜kPB^{GL(\Bbbk^{k})}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle-[\lambda]}}{{\longrightarrow}}VB^{k}_{\Bbbk} is sometimes called the associated vector bundle construction.

Remark 1.1.9.

One could argue that V​B𝕜kVB_{\Bbbk}^{k} is not the right category to study when discussing vector bundles, since we would also like to consider maps that are not invertible on the fibre. One could advocate that the statement of the equivalence of categories between V​B𝕜kVB_{\Bbbk}^{k} and P​BG​L​(𝕜k)PB^{GL(\Bbbk^{k})}  could be restricted to the statement that we have a bijective correspondence on objects. However, this equivalence of categories tells us more. It tells us that this bijective correspondence is natural with respect to a set of morphisms of vector bundles (and principal bundles), which includes the isomorphisms. Note that in the case in which we only consider the corresponding categories of bundles over a manifold MM with morphisms that are the identity (or some automorphism) on MM, this set of arrows consists precisely of the isomorphisms.

1.1.7 Orthogonal Frame Bundles

We can also start with a vector bundle equipped with a metric, i.e. a smooth fibrewise symmetric bilinear form (or Hermitian form in the complex case) gg that is non-degenerate in the sense that it identifies each fibre with its dual (antilinearly in the Hermitian case). This is a situation that we encounter all the time in physics. gg can either be a Euclidean, Hermitian, or Lorentzian metric. The examples are numerous. In these physical examples, we are usually not so much interested in the category of all vector bundles, but in the category M​V​B𝕜,(p,q)kMVB_{\Bbbk,(p,q)}^{k} of metrised kk-dimensional vector bundles over the field 𝕜\Bbbk with signature (p,q)(p,q). Of course, its objects are just kk-vector bundles together with a specified (p,q)(p,q)-metric while its arrows are vector bundle morphisms which are also isometries. (Note that isometries between kk-vector spaces are automatically invertible, so these morphisms are indeed fibrewise invertible.) We can equivalently describe these metrised vector bundles in the following way.

Claim 1.1.10.

Let O⁡(𝕜,(p,q))×𝕜k⟶λ𝕜kO(\Bbbk,(p,q))\times\Bbbk^{k}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\lambda}}{{\longrightarrow}}\Bbbk^{k} be the standard action of the orthogonal group corresponding to the standard (p,q)(p,q)-inner product ⟨⋅,⋅⟩\langle\>\cdot\,,\cdot\>\rangle on 𝕜k\Bbbk^{k}. Then we have an isomorphism of categories

Proof.

We first construct a metrisation functor MkM^{k}. Let ℱ:=(π,[Uα,ψα,gα​β])∈F​Bλ\mathcal{F}:=(\pi,[U_{\alpha},\psi_{\alpha},g_{\alpha\beta}])\in FB^{\lambda} be an (O⁡(𝕜,(p,q)),λ)(O(\Bbbk,(p,q)),\lambda)-fibre bundle (which is of course a vector bundle). Pick the corresponding maximal atlas structure, i.e. Σλ​(ℱ)=(π,(Uα,ψα,gα​β))\Sigma^{\lambda}(\mathcal{F})=(\pi,(U_{\alpha},\psi_{\alpha},g_{\alpha\beta})). Then each ψα\psi_{\alpha} gives us a (pseudo) inner product gαg_{\alpha} on π−1​(Uα)\pi^{-1}(U_{\alpha}) (from the standard inner product on 𝕜k\Bbbk^{k}). Moreover, these inner products agree on chart overlaps, since the transition functions act by the standard action of the orthogonal group. The sheaf property of smooth functions gives us a unique inner product gg on π\pi. We write Mk​(ℱ):=(ℱ,g)M^{k}(\mathcal{F}):=(\mathcal{F},g) for the metrised vector bundle we have constructed. Note that arrows in F​BλFB^{\lambda} are indeed isometries. Indeed, in charts, they are described by an action of the orthogonal group, so we can define MkM^{k} to be the identity on maps.

The demetrisation functor DkD^{k} will just be the functor that forgets the metric and is the identity on arrows. However, we have to show that a metrised vector bundle has an atlas with transition functions that only take values in O⁡(𝕜,(p,q))⊂G​L​(𝕜k)O(\Bbbk,(p,q))\subset GL(\Bbbk^{k}). This is obvious when we see that we can construct local orthonormal frames for the bundle.

Indeed, let (V⟶πM,g)(V\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\pi}}{{\longrightarrow}}M,g) be a metrised vector bundle. Let (Uα,ψα,gα​β)(U_{\alpha},\psi_{\alpha},g_{\alpha\beta}) be its maximal vector bundle atlas (so (gα​β)(g_{\alpha\beta}) have values in G​L​(𝕜k)GL(\Bbbk^{k})). Let (fα,j)(f_{\alpha,j}), Uα⟶fα,jV|UαU_{\alpha}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle f_{\alpha,j}}}{{\longrightarrow}}V|_{U_{\alpha}} be a local frame for V⟶πMV\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\pi}}{{\longrightarrow}}M. After refining the cover if necessary, the pointwise application of the Gram-Schmidt procedure gives us an orthonormal frame (fα,j′)(f^{\prime}_{\alpha,j}), i.e. a frame such that g⁡(fα,j′​(m),fα,k′​(m))=0g(f^{\prime}_{\alpha,j}(m),f^{\prime}_{\alpha,k}(m))=0 if j≠kj\neq k and g⁡(fα,j′​(m),fα,j′​(m))=±1g(f^{\prime}_{\alpha,j}(m),f^{\prime}_{\alpha,j}(m))=\pm 1, where the −--sign occurs when j≤pj\leq p and the ++-sign holds for the other qq indices. Of course, these orthonormal frames define a strictly equivalent atlas (Uα,ψα′,gα​β′)(U_{\alpha},\psi^{\prime}_{\alpha},g^{\prime}_{\alpha\beta}), by ψα′−1​(m,(v1,…,vk)):=∑j=1kvj​fα,j′​(m)\psi^{\prime-1}_{\alpha}(m,(v^{1},\ldots,v^{k})):=\sum_{j=1}^{k}v^{j}f_{\alpha,j}^{\prime}(m). Then, clearly, ⟨v,w⟩=g(ψα′(m,v)−1,ψα′(m,w)−1)\langle\>v\,,w\>\rangle=g(\psi^{\prime}_{\alpha}{}^{-1}(m,v),\psi^{\prime}_{\alpha}{}^{-1}(m,w)), where ⟨⋅,⋅⟩\langle\>\cdot\,,\cdot\>\rangle is the (p,q)(p,q)-inner product on 𝕜k\Bbbk^{k}. It follows that

⟨v,w⟩\displaystyle\langle\>v\,,w\>\rangle =g(ψβ′(m,v)−1,ψβ′(m,w)−1)\displaystyle=g(\psi^{\prime}_{\beta}{}^{-1}(m,v),\psi^{\prime}_{\beta}{}^{-1}(m,w))
=g(ψα′(m,gα​β′(m)⋅v)−1,ψα′(m,gα​β′(m)⋅w)−1)\displaystyle=g(\psi^{\prime}_{\alpha}{}^{-1}(m,g^{\prime}_{\alpha\beta}(m)\cdot v),\psi^{\prime}_{\alpha}{}^{-1}(m,g^{\prime}_{\alpha\beta}(m)\cdot w))
=⟨gα​β′​(m)⋅v,gα​β′​(m)⋅w⟩.\displaystyle=\langle\>g^{\prime}_{\alpha\beta}(m)\cdot v\,,g^{\prime}_{\alpha\beta}(m)\cdot w\>\rangle.

We conclude that the image of gα​β′g^{\prime}_{\alpha\beta} lies in O⁡(𝕜,(p,q))O(\Bbbk,(p,q)). This proves the claim, since MkM^{k} and DkD^{k} are clearly each other’s inverse. ∎

Remark 1.1.11.

Since we can construct a Riemannian metric on each vector bundle by using partitions of unity, we see that we can always specify a kk-dimensional vector bundle over 𝕜\Bbbk by transition functions with values in O⁡(𝕜,(k,0))O(\Bbbk,(k,0)). Put differently, by choosing a metric, we can interpret it as a (O⁡(𝕜,(k,0)),λ)(O(\Bbbk,(k,0)),\lambda)-fibre bundle. Note that this interpretation is highly non-canonical, depending on the choice of a metric.

Corollary 1.1.12.

Now, theorem 1.1.3 tells us that we obtain an equivalence of categories

M​V​B𝕜,(p,q)k⇆P​BO⁡(𝕜,(p,q)).MVB_{\Bbbk,(p,q)}^{k}\mathop{\leftrightarrows}PB^{O(\Bbbk,(p,q))}.

Similarly, we obtain an equivalence of categories

O​M​V​B𝕜,(p,q)k⇆P​BS​O​(𝕜,(p,q))OMVB_{\Bbbk,(p,q)}^{k}\mathop{\leftrightarrows}PB^{SO(\Bbbk,(p,q))}

between the categories O​M​V​B𝕜,(p,q)kOMVB_{\Bbbk,(p,q)}^{k} of oriented (p,q)(p,q)-metrised kk-vector bundles and that of S​O​(𝕜,(p,q))SO(\Bbbk,(p,q))-principal bundles1010 10 Here S​O​(𝕜,(p,q))SO(\Bbbk,(p,q)) is the subgroup of orientation-preserving elements of O⁡(𝕜,(p,q))O(\Bbbk,(p,q)) (those with determinant +1+1). Of course, in this somewhat clumsy notation, U⁡(n)=O⁡(ℂ,(n,0))U(n)=O(\mathbb{C}\;\,,(n,0)) and O⁡(p,q)=O⁡(ℝ,(p,q))O(p,q)=O(\mathbb{R}\,,(p,q)) and similarly for their orientation-preserving counterparts.

An important advantage of using an orthonormal frame bundle instead of a general frame bundle when describing physics is that its structure group GG is in many cases (in the case of a positive definite metric) compact. This means, for example, that, using the Haar measure, we can integrate over it to average quantities, making them invariant under the principal right action. Since the principal right action represents a change of basis, or gauge transformation, in the original vector bundle, this can be an important demand for quantities that are of physical interest. Moreover, in a very similar way, it will allow us to define invariant inner products on vector spaces on which we have a linear GG-action (in particular an Ad\mathrm{Ad}-invariant inner product on 𝔤\mathfrak{g}), which will be crucial ingredients in Yang-Mills theories.

This turns out to be a very useful way of looking at these bundles. Indeed, modern classical field theory is not formulated in the language of metrised vector bundles but in that of principal bundles with orthogonal structure groups. For example, the electromagnetic force is dealt with on a principal U⁡(1)U(1)-bundle, the weak force on a principal S​U​(2)SU(2)-bundle and the strong force on a principal S​U​(3)SU(3)-bundle. [13] Moreover, the spacetime metric in general relativity gives rise to an O⁡(1,3)O(1,3)-principal bundle that has the Lorentz frames as elements. Using this principal bundle, we can hope to define spinors on a curved spacetime, a construction that would be incomprehensible without the language of principal bundles.

Remark 1.1.13.

Of course, we never used the symmetry of the inner product in the proof of claim 1.1.10. A similar result therefore also holds, for example, for symplectic forms: the category of 2​k2k-dimensional symplectic vector bundles and the category of principal bundles with S​p​(2​k,𝕜)Sp(2k,\Bbbk) as a structure group are equivalent. One encounters an example of this fact when one constructs the (two-dimensional) spinor bundle corresponding to a spin structure on a manifold. Since this is an associated bundle to a S​L​(2,ℂ)SL(2,\mathbb{C}\;)-principal bundle and S​L​(2,ℂ)=S​p​(2,ℂ)SL(2,\mathbb{C}\;)=Sp(2,\mathbb{C}\;), we naturally obtain a symplectic form on the spinor bundle, from the canonical symplectic form on ℂ2\mathbb{C}\;^{2}. This symplectic form is used intensively by physicists, since it is closely related to the spacetime metric in general relativity, when we consider spin structures on a spacetime manifold.

1.1.8 How do sections transform under the equivalence?

In field theories, e.g. classical electromagnetism, physical quantities are described by sections of certain vector bundles over spacetime. While doing physics, we like to do calculations in concrete situations to derive concrete results. To do this, it is very convenient to drop the abstract notation we have been using, to pick a basis for each fibre and do the calculations in coordinates corresponding to this basis. Of course, we want this basis to vary smoothly with the base point. So, briefly, we pick a local frame for our vector bundle when we want to do computations.

This is where the frame bundle comes in. A local frame is, of course, just a local section of the frame bundle. So we have a natural idea of how sections of principal G​L​(𝕜k)GL(\Bbbk^{k})-bundles should transform under the equivalence of categories: they correspond to frames of the canonical associated bundle.

The converse question also naturally arises. The quantities of physical interest are sections of a vector bundle. If we want to describe the physics in terms of the corresponding frame bundle, we would like to know what the counterparts of these sections are in this context. The answer (in a slightly more general context) turns out to be as follows.

Claim 1.1.14.

Let (P,π,M,G)(P,\pi,M,G) be a principal fibre bundle and let G×S⟶λSG\times S\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\lambda}}{{\longrightarrow}}S be an effective action. Denote by C∞​(P,S)GC^{\infty}(P,S)^{G} the space of GG-equivariant mappings in the sense that Φ⁡(p⋅g)=g−1⋅Φ⁡(p)\Phi(p\cdot g)=g^{-1}\cdot\Phi(p) for all g∈Gg\in G, p∈Pp\in P and Φ∈C∞​(P,S)G\Phi\in C^{\infty}(P,S)^{G}. Then, sections σ∈Γ⁡(P⁡[λ])\sigma\in\Gamma(P[\lambda]) of the associated bundle are in one-to-one correspondence with GG-equivariant mappings Φ∈C∞​(P,S)G\Phi\in C^{\infty}(P,S)^{G}.

Proof.

Let Φ∈C∞​(P,S)G\Phi\in C^{\infty}(P,S)^{G}. Then we define a section σΦ\sigma_{\Phi} of the associated bundle as follows. Obviously P⟶idP×ΦP×SP\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathrm{id}_{P}\times\Phi}}{{\longrightarrow}}P\times S is GG-equivariant. Taking the quotient by the GG-action we obtain a smooth section σΦ=(idP×Φ)/G:M≅P/G⟶(P×S)/G=P⁡[λ]\sigma_{\Phi}=(\mathrm{id}_{P}\times\Phi)/G:M\cong P/G\stackrel{{\scriptstyle}}{{\longrightarrow}}(P\times S)/G=P[\lambda]. More explicitly, σΦ​(m):=[p,Φ⁡(p)]\sigma_{\Phi}(m):=[p,\Phi(p)], where p∈π~−1​(m)p\in\tilde{\pi}^{-1}(m). This expression is well-defined, for if π~​(p)=π~​(q)∈M\tilde{\pi}(p)=\tilde{\pi}(q)\in M, then there exists a g∈Gg\in G such that q=p⋅gq=p\cdot g. Then [q,Φ⁡(q)]=[p⋅g,Φ⁡(p⋅g)]=[p⋅g,g−1​Φ​(p)]=[p,Φ⁡(p)][q,\Phi(q)]=[p\cdot g,\Phi(p\cdot g)]=[p\cdot g,g^{-1}\Phi(p)]=[p,\Phi(p)], where the second equality holds since Φ\Phi is GG-equivariant. Moreover, we see that σΦ\sigma_{\Phi} is indeed a section of P⁡[λ]P[\lambda]. Further, σΦ∘π~=q∘(idP×Φ)\sigma_{\Phi}\circ\tilde{\pi}=q\circ(\mathrm{id}_{P}\times\Phi) and thus smooth, where P×S⟶qP⁡[λ]P\times S\stackrel{{\scriptstyle q}}{{\longrightarrow}}P[\lambda] is the quotient map. Since π~\tilde{\pi} is a surjective submersion, σΦ\sigma_{\Phi} is smooth as well.

Conversely, given σ∈Γ⁡(P⁡[λ])\sigma\in\Gamma(P[\lambda]), we define Φσ∈C∞​(P,S)G\Phi_{\sigma}\in C^{\infty}(P,S)^{G} by Φσ​(p):=qp−1​(σ⁡(π~​(p)))\Phi_{\sigma}(p):=q_{p}^{-1}(\sigma(\tilde{\pi}(p))), qpq_{p} is the restriction of qq, as in claim 1.1.5. Indeed, qp​(s)=[p,s]=[p⋅g,g−1⋅s]=qp⋅g​(g−1⋅s)q_{p}(s)=[p,s]=[p\cdot g,g^{-1}\cdot s]=q_{p\cdot g}(g^{-1}\cdot s) and therefore Φσ​(p⋅g)=qp⋅g−1​(σ⁡(m))=qp⋅g−1​(qp​(Φσ​(p)))=g−1⋅Φσ​(p)\Phi_{\sigma}(p\cdot g)=q_{p\cdot g}^{-1}(\sigma(m))=q_{p\cdot g}^{-1}(q_{p}(\Phi_{\sigma}(p)))=g^{-1}\cdot\Phi_{\sigma}(p). Smoothness of Φσ\Phi_{\sigma} is also apparent, if we note that Φσ​(p)=qp−1​(σ⁡(π~​(p)))=τ⁡(p,σ⁡(π~​(p)))\Phi_{\sigma}(p)=q_{p}^{-1}(\sigma(\tilde{\pi}(p)))=\tau(p,\sigma(\tilde{\pi}(p))), where τ\tau is the smooth map defined in claim 1.1.5.

ΦσΦ​(p)=qp−1​(σΦ​(π~​(p)))=qp−1​([p,Φ⁡(p)])=Φ⁡(p)and\Phi_{\sigma_{\Phi}}(p)=q_{p}^{-1}(\sigma_{\Phi}(\tilde{\pi}(p)))=q_{p}^{-1}([p,\Phi(p)])=\Phi(p)\quad\textnormal{and}\quad

∎

This is of course what physicists do all the time: they choose a local frame e∈Γ⁡(Fλ​(V)|U)e\in\Gamma(F^{\lambda}(V)|_{U}) for a vector bundle V⟶MV\stackrel{{\scriptstyle}}{{\longrightarrow}}M and identify a section σ∈Γ⁡(V)\sigma\in\Gamma(V) with its coordinates M⊃U⟶Φσ∘e𝕜kM\supset U\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\Phi_{\sigma}\circ e}}{{\longrightarrow}}\Bbbk^{k} with respect to the frame ee. Claim 1.1.14 tells us that this identification is valid.

This approach has the advantage that it is very concrete: a section of VV becomes just a function from MM that has some numbers as output, which enables us to do computations. However, we must always remember that the quantity Φσ∘e\Phi_{\sigma}\circ e is not an intrinsic characterisation of σ\sigma (Φσ\Phi_{\sigma} is though!), since it depends on the frame we choose to describe σ\sigma.

Remark 1.1.15.

In the theory of relativity, this principle has some remarkable manifestations. For example, the electromagnetic field is represented mathematically by a 22-form M⟶F⋀2T∗​MM\stackrel{{\scriptstyle F}}{{\longrightarrow}}\bigwedge^{2}T^{*}M on the spacetime manifold MM. An observer has an associated coordinate frame e∈Fλ​(V)|Ue\in F^{\lambda}(V)|_{U}, with eμ​ν=d​xμ∧d​xνe_{\mu\nu}=dx^{\mu}\wedge dx^{\nu}, if (xμ)(x^{\mu}) are geodesic normal coordinates in which the observer is at rest. With respect to this frame, we can describe FF in coordinates M⟶ΦF∘e=(Fμ​ν)⋀2(ℝ4)∗M\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\Phi_{F}\circ e=(F_{\mu\nu})}}{{\longrightarrow}}\bigwedge^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{4})^{*}. However, another observer will have their own coordinate frame e′e^{\prime} and with respect to this frame FF will have different coordinates (Fμ​ν′)(F_{\mu\nu}^{\prime}). Components of FF that one observer would describe as magnetic fields will be electric fields for the other and vice versa.

1.1.9 Categories of Principal Bundles Revisited

Principal bundles have turned out to play a fundamental role in modern physics. It is therefore important to stop and consider their properties.

There is some ambiguity when dealing with principal bundles from a categorical point of view. Of course, everyone would agree on what we would like to call a principal bundle. However, what maps should we consider? We have two choices to make:

  1. 1.

    Do we allow different base spaces MM (in which case it seems natural to allow the maps to be non-trivial on the base)?

  2. 2.

    Do we allow different structure groups GG (in which case it seems natural to allow the maps to be non-trivial on the group)?

This gives us our four categories of principal bundles, which turn out to be very useful: of course there is the biggest one, P​BPB, where we allow everything to happen, then there is P​BGPB^{G} (the one of [15]), where the answers to the questions are, respectively, yes and no, P​BMPB_{M} (the one of [18]), where the answers are the other way around, and finally P​BMGPB_{M}^{G}, where we answer no to both questions. The first category is essential when we want to emphasise the role of a principal bundle as a special case of a (G,λ)(G,\lambda)-fibre bundle. On the other hand, the second two are more workable when we want to do physics. In particular, we have the following results that will be important for gauge theory.

Claim 1.1.16.

P​BMPB_{M} has finite products. To be precise, if Pi⟶π~iMP_{i}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\tilde{\pi}_{i}}}{{\longrightarrow}}M is a principal GiG_{i}-bundle, then the fibred product P1×MP2⟶π~MP_{1}\times_{M}P_{2}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\tilde{\pi}}}{{\longrightarrow}}M is a principal G1×G2G_{1}\times G_{2}-bundle. This is the categorical product.

Proof.

We take the projection from π~\tilde{\pi} to π~i\tilde{\pi}_{i} to be the map of principal bundles that is the obvious projection onto the ii-th component as a map of fibre bundles and the projection G1×G2⟶GiG_{1}\times G_{2}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle}}{{\longrightarrow}}G_{i} on the structure group. The universal property of the product is easily checked. ∎

It should be noted that physicists usually call π~\tilde{\pi} the spliced principal bundle of π~1\tilde{\pi}_{1} and π~2\tilde{\pi}_{2}. 1111 11 Although the importance of this construction might not be evident from this thesis, it is one of the more important tools in gauge theory. When we deal with particles that interact with multiple gauge fields or with particles with spin, the construction is essential to obtain the correct principal bundle on which the physics is described.

The following is a definition that is of the most fundamental importance in gauge theory.

Definition.

Let P⟶π~M∈P​BMGP\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\tilde{\pi}}}{{\longrightarrow}}M\in PB^{G}_{M} be a principal GG-bundle. We call Aut⁡(π~)\mathrm{Aut}(\tilde{\pi}), the group of automorphisms of π~\tilde{\pi} in P​BMGPB^{G}_{M}, the group of gauge transformations of π~\tilde{\pi} and denote it by Gau⁡(π~)\mathrm{Gau}(\tilde{\pi}). To be explicit, this group consists of diffeomorphisms P⟶kPP\stackrel{{\scriptstyle k}}{{\longrightarrow}}P, such that π~∘k=π~\tilde{\pi}\circ k=\tilde{\pi} and such that ρg∘k=k∘ρg\rho_{g}\circ k=k\circ\rho_{g}, for all g∈Gg\in G. Note that any arrow in P​BMGPB^{G}_{M} is an isomorphism, so Gau​π~\mathrm{Gau}\,\tilde{\pi} consists precisely of the endomorphisms of π~\tilde{\pi} in P​BMGPB^{G}_{M}.

Just like Diff​S\mathrm{Diff}\,S, Gau​π~\mathrm{Gau}\,\tilde{\pi} has the structure of an infinite-dimensional manifold on which the group operations are smooth. [22] In the line of thought of the previous paragraph, we have the following result.

Claim 1.1.17.

There is an isomorphism of groups C∞​(P,G)G≅Gau​π~C^{\infty}(P,G)^{G}\cong\mathrm{Gau}\,\tilde{\pi}, where we take GG to act on itself on the left by conjugation. Claim 1.1.14 now tells us that we can see gauge transformations as sections of the obvious associated (G,C)(G,C)-fibre bundle.

Proof.

Let Φ∈C∞​(P,G)G\Phi\in C^{\infty}(P,G)^{G}. Then we define a map P⟶kΦPP\stackrel{{\scriptstyle k_{\Phi}}}{{\longrightarrow}}P by kΦ​(p):=p⋅Φ⁡(p)k_{\Phi}(p):=p\cdot\Phi(p). Obviously, this is a map of fibre bundles that is the identity on MM. Moreover kΦ​(p⋅g)=(p⋅g)⋅Φ⁡(p⋅g)=(p⋅g)⋅g−1⋅Φ⁡(p)⋅g=p⋅Φ⁡(p)⋅g=kΦ​(p)⋅gk_{\Phi}(p\cdot g)=(p\cdot g)\cdot\Phi(p\cdot g)=(p\cdot g)\cdot g^{-1}\cdot\Phi(p)\cdot g=p\cdot\Phi(p)\cdot g=k_{\Phi}(p)\cdot g, so kΦk_{\Phi} is a map of principal bundles that is the identity on GG. We conclude that kΦ∈Gau​π~k_{\Phi}\in\mathrm{Gau}\,\tilde{\pi}.

Conversely, let k∈Gau​π~k\in\mathrm{Gau}\,\tilde{\pi} and define P⟶ΦkGP\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\Phi_{k}}}{{\longrightarrow}}G by the implicit relation k⁡(p)=p⋅Φk​(p)k(p)=p\cdot\Phi_{k}(p). (Note that this is a good definition since the principal right action is transitive and free on the fibre. Moreover, smoothness is immediate from the smoothness of the group multiplication, if we write out the definition in a chart.) Now, p⋅g⋅Φk​(p⋅g)=k⁡(p⋅g)=k⁡(p)⋅g=p⋅Φk​(p)⋅gp\cdot g\cdot\Phi_{k}(p\cdot g)=k(p\cdot g)=k(p)\cdot g=p\cdot\Phi_{k}(p)\cdot g. Therefore Φk​(p⋅g)=g−1⋅Φk​(p)⋅g\Phi_{k}(p\cdot g)=g^{-1}\cdot\Phi_{k}(p)\cdot g. We conclude that Φk∈C∞​(P,G)G\Phi_{k}\in C^{\infty}(P,G)^{G}.

Now, obviously, these constructions are each other’s inverse. Finally, let Φ,Φ′∈C∞​(P,G)G\Phi,\Phi^{\prime}\in C^{\infty}(P,G)^{G}. Then kΦ∘kΦ′​(p)=p⋅Φ′​(p)⋅Φ⁡(p⋅Φ′​(p))=p⋅Φ′​(p)⋅Φ′​(p)−1⋅Φ⁡(p)⋅Φ′​(p)=p⋅Φ⁡(p)⋅Φ′​(p)=kΦ⋅Φ′​(p)k_{\Phi}\circ k_{\Phi^{\prime}}(p)=p\cdot\Phi^{\prime}(p)\cdot\Phi(p\cdot\Phi^{\prime}(p))=p\cdot\Phi^{\prime}(p)\cdot\Phi^{\prime}(p)^{-1}\cdot\Phi(p)\cdot\Phi^{\prime}(p)=p\cdot\Phi(p)\cdot\Phi^{\prime}(p)=k_{\Phi\cdot\Phi^{\prime}}(p). ∎

Remark 1.1.18.

These gauge transformations are a generalisation to arbitrary spacetimes of what physicists call gauge transformations. Indeed, every principal bundle over Minkowski spacetime M=ℝ4M=\mathbb{R}^{4} is trivial, since ℝ4\mathbb{R}^{4} is contractible. [28] Therefore, in the case of a principal GG-bundle π~\tilde{\pi} over M=ℝ4M=\mathbb{R}^{4} (which we know to be trivial), we can construct a special class of gauge transformations from maps M⟶ϕGM\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\phi}}{{\longrightarrow}}G, by defining fϕ∈Gau​π~f_{\phi}\in\mathrm{Gau}\,\tilde{\pi} by fϕ​(m,g)=(m,ϕ⁡(m)⋅g)f_{\phi}(m,g)=(m,\phi(m)\cdot g). Indeed, for a trivial principal bundle, we easily see that every gauge transformation is of this form. These transformations are what physicists call a local gauge transformation, in contrast to the case in which they demand that ϕ\phi be constant, in which case they talk about global gauge transformations. It is important to see, however, that in general, such a difference cannot be made and we can only talk about plain gauge transformations.

1.2 Connections on Fibre Bundles

In this section, I introduce the notion of a connection on a fibre bundle, which is central both in the general theory of relativity, where it determines the geodesics along which a point particle moves through spacetime (and in some sense is a potential for the gravitational field), and in elementary particle physics, where it describes the gauge potentials, the mathematical abstractions of the fundamental interactions of matter.

Many different notions of a connection are used in the literature. I will use a particularly general geometric definition, in accordance with [19], and will treat a few special cases separately. I hope that this abstract approach will help the reader to see the connections between the mathematics used in the different theories of physics, which are insufficiently emphasised in many references.

1.2.1 A Geometric Definition

Let F⟶πMF\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\pi}}{{\longrightarrow}}M be a fibre bundle. Note that at each point f∈Ff\in F the kernel ker⁡Tf​π\ker T_{f}\pi is a linear subspace of Tf​FT_{f}F. This is easily seen to define a subbundle ker⁡T​π⊂T​F\ker T\pi\subset TF over FF, called the vertical bundle and denoted V​FVF.

This bundle can also be given another interpretation. To see this, note that

0⟶Tf​Fm⟶Tf​imTf​F⟶Tf​πTm​M⟶00\stackrel{{\scriptstyle}}{{\longrightarrow}}T_{f}F_{m}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle T_{f}i_{m}}}{{\longrightarrow}}T_{f}F\stackrel{{\scriptstyle T_{f}\pi}}{{\longrightarrow}}T_{m}M\stackrel{{\scriptstyle}}{{\longrightarrow}}0

is a short exact sequence. Here m=π⁡(f)m=\pi(f) and Fm⟶imFF_{m}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle i_{m}}}{{\longrightarrow}}F denotes the inclusion. (Indeed π∘im\pi\circ i_{m} has constant value m, so im​Tf​im⊂V​Ff\mathrm{im}\;T_{f}i_{m}\subset VF_{f}. Moreover their dimensions are equal.) 1212 12 Furthermore, if FF is a vector bundle, we can identify Tf​Fm≅FmT_{f}F_{m}\cong F_{m}, so, in that case, we can see the vertical subspace V​FfVF_{f} at a point ff as a copy of FmF_{m}. The short exact sequence above also tells us that we can identify the quotient space Tf​F/V​FfT_{f}F/VF_{f} with Tm​MT_{m}M. This gives us the following identity of vector bundles over FF:

T​F/V​F≅π∗​T​M,TF/VF\cong\pi^{*}TM,

where π∗​T​M\pi^{*}TM denotes the pullback bundle of T​MTM along π\pi. Of course, this calls for an explicit realisation of T​FTF as a direct sum of V​FVF and π∗​T​M\pi^{*}TM. This is given by a connection.

Definition (Connection).

Let F⟶πMF\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\pi}}{{\longrightarrow}}M be a fibre bundle. Although I will interchangeably use the vertical projection PVP_{V} and the horizontal bundle H​FHF to denote a connection, what I mean by a connection is the whole product diagram H​F⟵PHT​F⟶PVV​FHF\stackrel{{\scriptstyle P_{H}}}{{\longleftarrow}}TF\stackrel{{\scriptstyle P_{V}}}{{\longrightarrow}}VF in the category F​BFFB_{F} of fibre bundles over FF.

1.2.5 The Pullback

The pullback is an essential tool when working with fibre bundles. It is a well-known fact that the categorical pullback of a fibre bundle along an arbitrary map exists in the smooth category. This follows from the fact that a fibre bundle is a submersion and therefore transversal to any map1313 13 Remember that a pair of maps M1⟶f1NM_{1}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle f_{1}}}{{\longrightarrow}}N, M2⟶f2NM_{2}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle f_{2}}}{{\longrightarrow}}N is said to be transversal if im​Tm1​f1+im​Tm2​f2=Tn​N\mathrm{im}\;T_{m_{1}}f_{1}+\mathrm{im}\;T_{m_{2}}f_{2}=T_{n}N for every triple (m1,m2,n=f1(m1)=f2(m2))∈M1×M2×N(m_{1},m_{2},n=f_{1}(m_{1})=f_{2}(m_{2}))\in M_{1}\times M_{2}\times N. It is a direct consequence of the submersion theorem that the topological pullback of a pair of transversal maps is a smooth submanifold of M1×M2M_{1}\times M_{2}.. 1.2.6 Parallel Transport

As noted above, there are many different (more or less) equivalent definitions of connections. I find one approach to be particularly intuitive, much more so than the one I have taken so far. It can be argued that a connection should be viewed as a rule that identifies fibres of a fibre bundle along paths in the base space MM. This identification is called parallel transport.

I will show how to derive a rule for parallel transport from our definition of a connection. Moreover, it can be shown that the connection can be recovered from its parallel transport. (See [10].) Apart from being a very intuitive approach to connections and being a very practical tool in, say, general relativity, this definition generalises well to higher categorical analogues of fibre bundles (which appear in higher gauge theory). (See [26].)

In section 1.2.3, we have seen that we can construct a unique horizontal lift Xhor∈𝒳⁡(F)X_{\mathrm{hor}}\in\mathcal{X}(F) for each vector field X∈𝒳⁡(M)X\in\mathcal{X}(M). This is by lifting each vector pointwise. Suppose we are given a curve ]a,b[⟶cM]a,b[\stackrel{{\scriptstyle c}}{{\longrightarrow}}M. Notice that the tangent vectors to this curve are elements of T​MTM and can therefore be uniquely lifted to vectors in H​F⊂T​FHF\subset TF. We can ask whether these vectors give rise to a (local) curve in FF. The answer is the following.

1.2.7 Complete Connections and Holonomy

Unfortunately, the existence of parallel transport is only proved locally by theorem 1.2.9. Global transport might not be possible for all connections. However, many useful connections allow global parallel transport. Principal connections and affine connections, with the Levi-Civita connections of a (pseudo)-Riemannian manifold, come to mind. Such connections are said to be complete.

Now, it is easily verified that, in the proof of theorem 1.2.9, we only needed cc to be a piecewise-C1C^{1}-curve1414 14 It can be shown that one can equivalently take the curves to be CkC^{k}, for any k∈ℕ>0k\in\mathbb{N}_{>0}, or even C∞C^{\infty}. [18]. Thus, for a complete connection, parallel transport along piecewise-C1C^{1} loops based at m∈Mm\in M assigns to each such loop a diffeomorphism of the fibre FmF_{m}:

This assignment is compatible with concatenation and reversal of paths, so its image is a subgroup of Diff⁡(Fm)\mathrm{Diff}(F_{m}), known as the holonomy group at mm. This group is a useful tool for classification of fibre bundles with connections, (pseudo)-Riemannian manifolds with the Levi-Civita connection being an important example.

1.2.8 Curvature as Infinitesimal Holonomy

We have seen that holonomy cannot be defined for arbitrary connections, since the parallel transport might not be globally defined along any loop. However, if we make the loops small enough, one would expect that the transport would be possible. Here, ”small enough” will mean infinitesimal. We will see that this infinitesimal transport is nothing but the curvature, which, indeed, is defined for any connection.

The following result, in some sense, tells us that we can view the curvature as a limit of the holonomy if we take smaller and smaller loops. (We take loops corresponding to two commuting vector fields, or equivalently (by Frobenius), two local coordinate vector fields.)

Claim 1.2.10 (Curvature as infinitesimal holonomy).

If X,Y∈𝒳⁡(M)X,Y\in\mathcal{X}(M) are two commuting vector fields, we have that

−R⁡(X,Y)​(f)=∂2∂s​∂t​(e−t​Yhor∘e−s​Xhor∘et​Yhor∘es​Xhor​(f))|s=t=0.-R(X,Y)(f)=\frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial s\partial t}\left(e^{-tY_{\mathrm{hor}}}\circ e^{-sX_{\mathrm{hor}}}\circ e^{tY_{\mathrm{hor}}}\circ e^{sX_{\mathrm{hor}}}(f)\right)\Big|_{s=t=0}.
Proof.

We have already derived formula 1.1, which expresses the curvature in terms of the horizontal lifts of XX and YY. If [X,Y]=0[X,Y]=0, this reduces to the equality

−R⁡(X,Y)​(f)=[Xhor,Yhor]​(f).-R(X,Y)(f)=[X_{\mathrm{hor}},Y_{\mathrm{hor}}](f).

The claim follows by using the following well-known identity for the bracket of two vector fields:

[Xhor,Yhor]​(f)=∂2∂s​∂t​(e−t​Yhor∘e−s​Xhor∘et​Yhor∘es​Xhor​(f))|s=t=0.[X_{\mathrm{hor}},Y_{\mathrm{hor}}](f)=\frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial s\partial t}\left(e^{-tY_{\mathrm{hor}}}\circ e^{-sX_{\mathrm{hor}}}\circ e^{tY_{\mathrm{hor}}}\circ e^{sX_{\mathrm{hor}}}(f)\right)\Big|_{s=t=0}.

∎

1.3 Connections on Principal Bundles

Suppose that P⟶π~MP\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\tilde{\pi}}}{{\longrightarrow}}M is a principal GG-bundle. We ask ourselves what a good notion of a connection on a principal bundle is. GG-equivariant connections turn out to be particularly interesting. Later, we will see that, in the case G=G​L​(𝕜k)G=GL(\Bbbk^{k}), precisely these connections correspond to the ordinary affine connections on the canonical associated vector bundle P⁡[λ]P[\lambda]. In this sense, they are a generalisation of affine connections to general principal bundles. Before we explain the precise condition of equivariance that we put on the connection, however, let us formulate another, more conventional way of looking at connections on principal bundles.

1.3.1 Principal Connection 1-forms

We note that the principal right action (which we write as ρ\rho) defines fundamental vector fields for the Lie algebra 𝔤\mathfrak{g} of GG as follows. For Z∈𝔤Z\in\mathfrak{g} and p∈Pp\in P, we write ZP​(p):=dd​t​ρexp⁡(t​Z)​(p)|t=0=T​ρp​(Z)Z_{P}(p):=\frac{d}{dt}\rho_{\exp(tZ)}(p)|_{t=0}=T\rho^{p}(Z), where G⟶ρpPG\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rho^{p}}}{{\longrightarrow}}P denotes the smooth map g↦ρ⁡(p,g)g\mapsto\rho(p,g). For a right action this assignment is a Lie-algebra homomorphism 𝔤⟶𝒳⁡(P)\mathfrak{g}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle}}{{\longrightarrow}}\mathcal{X}(P). Recall that, since the vertical bundle is integrable, Γ⁡(V​P)\Gamma(VP) forms a Lie subalgebra of 𝒳⁡(P)\mathcal{X}(P). Now, since the orbits of the principal right action are the fibres of PP, the same assignment gives a linear map 𝔤⟶Γ⁡(V​P)\mathfrak{g}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle}}{{\longrightarrow}}\Gamma(VP). Moreover, this map trivialises V​PVP.

The map

Proof.

ζ\zeta respects the fibre, since ZP​(p)∈V​PpZ_{P}(p)\in VP_{p}. (Put differently, ζ\zeta is the identity map on PP.) Linearity on each fibre follows because Z↦ZP​(p)=Te​ρp​(Z)Z\mapsto Z_{P}(p)=T_{e}\rho^{p}(Z) is linear:

(Z+λ​Z′)P​(p)=Te​ρp​(Z+λ​Z′)=ZP​(p)+λ​ZP′​(p).(Z+\lambda Z^{\prime})_{P}(p)=T_{e}\rho^{p}(Z+\lambda Z^{\prime})=Z_{P}(p)+\lambda Z^{\prime}_{P}(p).

Let p∈Pp\in P and let (U,ψ)(U,\psi) be a trivialisation of PP around pp.

Now, ζ⁡(p,Z)=T​ρp​(Z)\zeta(p,Z)=T\rho^{p}(Z). Note that ρp\rho^{p} is a diffeomorphism G⟶PpG\stackrel{{\scriptstyle}}{{\longrightarrow}}P_{p}. Therefore 𝔤=Te​G⟶Te​ρpTp​Pp=V​Pp\mathfrak{g}=T_{e}G\stackrel{{\scriptstyle T_{e}\rho^{p}}}{{\longrightarrow}}T_{p}P_{p}=VP_{p} is an isomorphism of vector spaces. ζ\zeta is obviously smooth, as ζ⁡(p,Z)=T​ρp​(Z)=T​ρ​(0p,Z)\zeta(p,Z)=T\rho^{p}(Z)=T\rho(0_{p},Z). There is a generalised notion of a differential form that is very useful in this situation. Let MM be a manifold and let V⟶πMV\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\pi}}{{\longrightarrow}}M be a vector bundle. We define a π\pi-valued differential kk-form on MM as a map η\eta of vector bundles1515 15 Note that we can equivalently view these π\pi-valued differential forms as sections of the vector bundle V⊗⋀kT∗​MV\otimes\bigwedge^{k}T^{*}M.:

Now, let us formulate what we mean precisely when we say that a connection is equivariant. We say that PP is equipped with a principal connection, or equivariant connection, if H​P⟵PHT​P⟶PVV​PHP\stackrel{{\scriptstyle P_{H}}}{{\longleftarrow}}TP\stackrel{{\scriptstyle P_{V}}}{{\longrightarrow}}VP is equivariant in the following sense: PV∘T⁡(ρg)=T⁡(ρg)∘PVP_{V}\circ T(\rho_{g})=T(\rho_{g})\circ P_{V}, for all g∈Gg\in G. (Here I write ρ(−)\rho_{(-)} for the principal right action to be explicit.) Note that we can equivalently demand that horizontal lifts are GG-equivariant or that parallel transport along any curve is. We must ask ourselves what it means for ω\omega, if we are dealing with a principal connection. The answer turns out to be as follows.

In general, given a representation λ\lambda of GG on a vector space WW, we say that α∈Ωk​(P,W)\alpha\in\Omega^{k}(P,W) is an equivariant differential form if α⁡(T​ρg​(X1),…,T​ρg​(Xk))=λ⁡(g−1)​α​(X1,…,Xk)\alpha(T\rho_{g}(X_{1}),\ldots,T\rho_{g}(X_{k}))=\lambda(g^{-1})\alpha(X_{1},\ldots,X_{k}), for all g∈Gg\in G.

Claim 1.3.5.

For a principal connection ω\omega on a principal bundle PP, ℒZPω=−ad(Z)∘ω\mathcal{L}_{Z_{P}}\omega=-\mathrm{ad}(Z)\circ\omega.

Proof.
