The bracket on 𝔤\mathfrak{g} defines a bracket on the graded vector space Ω⁡(M,𝔤):=⨁k∈ℕΩk​(M,𝔤)\Omega(M,\mathfrak{g}):=\bigoplus_{k\in\mathbb{N}}\Omega^{k}(M,\mathfrak{g}) of all 𝔤\mathfrak{g}-valued differential forms on a manifold MM, making it into a graded Lie algebra. For α∈Ωk​(M,𝔤)\alpha\in\Omega^{k}(M,\mathfrak{g}) and β∈Ωl​(M,𝔤)\beta\in\Omega^{l}(M,\mathfrak{g}), we define [α,β]∈Ωk+l​(M,𝔤)[\alpha,\beta]\in\Omega^{k+l}(M,\mathfrak{g}) by

[α,β]​(X1,…,Xk+l):=1k!​l!​∑σsign​σ​[α⁡(Xσ⁡(1),…,Xσ⁡(k)),β⁡(Xσ⁡(k+1),…,Xσ⁡(k+l))],[\alpha,\beta](X_{1},\ldots,X_{k+l}):=\frac{1}{k!l!}\sum_{\sigma}\mathrm{sign}\,\sigma[\alpha(X_{\sigma(1)},\ldots,X_{\sigma(k)}),\beta(X_{\sigma(k+1)},\ldots,X_{\sigma(k+l)})],

where σ\sigma ranges over all permutations of {1,…,k+l}\{1,\ldots,k+l\} and Xi∈T​MX_{i}\in TM.

The ordinary exterior derivative extends componentwise to 𝔤\mathfrak{g}-valued forms. For α∈Ωk​(M,𝔤)\alpha\in\Omega^{k}(M,\mathfrak{g}) and β∈Ωl​(M,𝔤)\beta\in\Omega^{l}(M,\mathfrak{g}) it satisfies the graded Leibniz rule

d⁡[α,β]=[d​α,β]+(−1)k​[α,d​β].d[\alpha,\beta]=[d\alpha,\beta]+(-1)^{k}[\alpha,d\beta].

For a 𝔤\mathfrak{g}-valued 11-form, d​ω​(X,Y):=ℒX​(ω⁡(Y))−ℒY​(ω⁡(X))−ω⁡([X,Y])d\omega(X,Y):=\mathcal{L}_{X}(\omega(Y))-\mathcal{L}_{Y}(\omega(X))-\omega([X,Y]). This implies that the following proposition holds for GG-equivariant connections.

First, however, we introduce one more notation that makes the proposition somewhat cleaner. Moreover, the notation is used in practically all physics literature on gauge theory. Recall that we used PHP_{H} to designate the projection onto the horizontal bundle. This allows us to define a map

Ω⁡(P,W)⟶PH∗Ω⁡(P,W)\Omega(P,W)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle P_{H}^{*}}}{{\longrightarrow}}\Omega(P,W)
(PH∗​α)​(X1,…,Xk):=α⁡(PH​(X1),…,PH​(Xk)).(P_{H}^{*}\alpha)(X_{1},\ldots,X_{k}):=\alpha(P_{H}(X_{1}),\ldots,P_{H}(X_{k})).

We might call this the projection onto the subspace Ωhor​(P,W)\Omega_{\mathrm{hor}}(P,W) of horizontal differential forms. Obviously, these are precisely the differential forms that vanish on vertical vectors. Finally, we define the exterior covariant derivative or covariant differential associated with the connection ω\omega as the map Ωk​(P,W)⟶dωΩk+1​(P,W)\Omega^{k}(P,W)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d^{\omega}}}{{\longrightarrow}}\Omega^{k+1}(P,W), given by dω:=PH∗∘dd^{\omega}:=P_{H}^{*}\circ d.

Theorem 1.3.6 (Cartan’s second structural equation).

For a principal connection ω\omega on PP the following formula holds for the curvature: Ωω=d​ω+12​[ω,ω]=dω​ω\Omega^{\omega}=d\omega+\frac{1}{2}[\omega,\omega]=d^{\omega}\omega.

Proof.

Let X,YX,Y be horizontal vector fields on PP. Then R⁡(X,Y):=−PV​([X,Y])=(−ω⁡([X,Y]))PR(X,Y):=-P_{V}([X,Y])=(-\omega([X,Y]))_{P} and

(d​ω+12​[ω,ω])​(X,Y)\displaystyle(d\omega+\frac{1}{2}[\omega,\omega])(X,Y) =ℒX​(ω⁡(Y))−ℒY​(ω⁡(X))−ω⁡([X,Y])+[ω⁡(X),ω⁡(Y)]\displaystyle=\mathcal{L}_{X}(\omega(Y))-\mathcal{L}_{Y}(\omega(X))-\omega([X,Y])+[\omega(X),\omega(Y)]
=−ω⁡([X,Y]),\displaystyle=-\omega([X,Y]),

since 0=PV​X=(ω⁡(X))P0=P_{V}X=(\omega(X))_{P} implies that ω⁡(X)=0\omega(X)=0 and similarly for YY. So on horizontal vector fields, both expressions agree.

Now note that, since the principal right action is transitive on the fibre, any vertical vector Z′∈V​PpZ^{\prime}\in VP_{p} can be written as ZP​(p)Z_{P}(p) for some Z∈𝔤Z\in\mathfrak{g}. Now, trivially, iZP​R=iPH​ZP​R=0i_{Z_{P}}R=i_{P_{H}Z_{P}}R=0, so iZP​Ωω=0i_{Z_{P}}\Omega^{\omega}=0.

On the other hand, since iZP​ω=Zi_{Z_{P}}\omega=Z, we have that iZP​d​ω=ℒZP​ωi_{Z_{P}}d\omega=\mathcal{L}_{Z_{P}}\omega. So

iZP​(d​ω+12​[ω,ω])\displaystyle i_{Z_{P}}(d\omega+\frac{1}{2}[\omega,\omega]) =ℒZP​ω+12​iZP​[ω,ω]\displaystyle=\mathcal{L}_{Z_{P}}\omega+\frac{1}{2}i_{Z_{P}}[\omega,\omega]
=ℒZP​ω+[Z,ω]\displaystyle=\mathcal{L}_{Z_{P}}\omega+[Z,\omega]

(We mean [Z,ω][Z,\omega] to be the pointwise 𝔤\mathfrak{g}-Lie bracket.) This last equality is the well-known result on the adjoint representation. Since ω\omega is GG-equivariant, claim 1.3.5 tells us that this vanishes. Both expressions therefore vanish on vertical vectors. By noting that both are C∞​(P)C^{\infty}(P)-bilinear maps, the first equality in the theorem follows.

For the second one, note that

dω​ω​(X∧Y)\displaystyle d^{\omega}\omega(X\wedge Y) =(PH∗​d​ω)​(X∧Y)\displaystyle=(P_{H}^{*}d\omega)(X\wedge Y)
=d​ω​(PH​(X)∧PH​(Y))\displaystyle=d\omega(P_{H}(X)\wedge P_{H}(Y))

=−ω([PH(X),PH(Y)])(since ω vanishes on horizontal vectors).\displaystyle=-\omega([P_{H}(X),P_{H}(Y)])\quad\textnormal{(since $\omega$ vanishes on horizontal vectors)}\quad.

Note that this expression is equal to −ω⁡([X,Y])-\omega([X,Y]) (and therefore agrees with the expression above) if X,YX,Y are horizontal vectors. Moreover it obviously vanishes on vertical vectors. We conclude that the second identity in the theorem holds. ∎

There is one more identity regarding the connection that I would like to show, since it is of fundamental importance in physics. It will give us one of the two equations governing the evolution of gauge fields.

Theorem 1.3.7 (Bianchi Identity).

The curvature form Ωω\Omega^{\omega} of a principal connection ω\omega satisfies the following equation, known as the Bianchi Identity:

dω​Ωω=0.d^{\omega}\Omega^{\omega}=0.
Proof.

We have, using the previous result,

dω​Ωω\displaystyle d^{\omega}\Omega^{\omega} =dω​(d​ω+12​[ω,ω])\displaystyle=d^{\omega}(d\omega+\frac{1}{2}[\omega,\omega])
=PH∗​d​d​ω+12​PH∗​d​[ω,ω]\displaystyle=P_{H}^{*}dd\omega+\frac{1}{2}P_{H}^{*}d[\omega,\omega]
=12​PH∗​([d​ω,ω]−[ω,d​ω])\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}P_{H}^{*}([d\omega,\omega]-[\omega,d\omega])
=PH∗​[d​ω,ω]\displaystyle=P_{H}^{*}[d\omega,\omega]
=[PH∗​d​ω,PH∗​ω]\displaystyle=[P_{H}^{*}d\omega,P_{H}^{*}\omega]
=0.\displaystyle=0.

The last identity, of course, holds since ω\omega vanishes on horizontal vectors. ∎

It should be noted that any connection on a fibre bundle satisfies a variant of this equation: it is not special to the case of a principal connection. However, the general statement would be much more involved. For more information, see [19].

To express the second field equation (known as the Yang-Mills equation) we need a few more definitions. Let us, following convention, first introduce the notation Ωhork​(P,W)G\Omega_{\mathrm{hor}}^{k}(P,W)^{G} for the space of WW-valued kk-forms that are both horizontal (vanish on vertical vectors) and equivariant. This is a very important class of differential forms. For instance, note that Ωω∈Ωhor2​(P,𝔤)G\Omega^{\omega}\in\Omega_{\mathrm{hor}}^{2}(P,\mathfrak{g})^{G}. We have a similar result for ω\omega.

Claim 1.3.8.

Let ω\omega be a principal connection on P⟶π~MP\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\tilde{\pi}}}{{\longrightarrow}}M. Then another ω′∈Ω1​(P,𝔤)\omega^{\prime}\in\Omega^{1}(P,\mathfrak{g}) is a principal connection precisely if ω−ω′∈Ωhor1​(P,𝔤)G\omega-\omega^{\prime}\in\Omega_{\mathrm{hor}}^{1}(P,\mathfrak{g})^{G}. Obviously, ω′\omega^{\prime} is precisely equivariant if ω−ω′\omega-\omega^{\prime} is. In fact, this is an (infinite-dimensional) submanifold of Ω1​(P,𝔤)\Omega^{1}(P,\mathfrak{g}). [6] We can interpret Ωhor1​(P,𝔤)G\Omega_{\mathrm{hor}}^{1}(P,\mathfrak{g})^{G} as its tangent space. Indeed, let ]−ϵ,ϵ[⟶γ𝒞(P)]-\epsilon,\epsilon[\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\gamma}}{{\longrightarrow}}\mathscr{C}(P) be a path. Then, γ⁡(t)=γ⁡(0)+δ⁡(t)\gamma(t)=\gamma(0)+\delta(t), with ]−ϵ,ϵ[⟶δΩhor1(P,𝔤)G]-\epsilon,\epsilon[\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\delta}}{{\longrightarrow}}\Omega_{\mathrm{hor}}^{1}(P,\mathfrak{g})^{G}. We see that γ′​(0)∈T0​Ωhor1​(P,𝔤)G≅Ωhor1​(P,𝔤)G\gamma^{\prime}(0)\in T_{0}\Omega_{\mathrm{hor}}^{1}(P,\mathfrak{g})^{G}\cong\Omega_{\mathrm{hor}}^{1}(P,\mathfrak{g})^{G}.

Remark 1.3.9.

I can imagine the definition of Ωhork​(P,W)G\Omega_{\mathrm{hor}}^{k}(P,W)^{G} can seem somewhat far-fetched. How precisely should we think about these differential forms? To answer this question note that, by claim 1.1.14, we have a natural identification Ωhor0​(P,W)G=C∞​(P,W)G≅Γ⁡(P⁡[λ])\Omega_{\mathrm{hor}}^{0}(P,W)^{G}=C^{\infty}(P,W)^{G}\cong\Gamma(P[\lambda]). Because of the identification H​Pp≅T​Mπ~​(p)HP_{p}\cong TM_{\tilde{\pi}(p)} given by the connection and the transitivity of the principal right action on the fibres of π~\tilde{\pi} we therefore obtain a natural identification Ωhork​(P,W)G≅Γ⁡(P⁡[λ]⊗⋀kT∗​M)≅Ωk​(M,P⁡[λ]⟶πM)\Omega_{\mathrm{hor}}^{k}(P,W)^{G}\cong\Gamma(P[\lambda]\otimes\bigwedge^{k}T^{*}M)\cong\Omega^{k}(M,P[\lambda]\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\pi}}{{\longrightarrow}}M).

If MM has an orientation, we can define a Hodge star operation on Ω⁡(M,π)\Omega(M,\pi). This can be transferred to Ωhor​(P,W)G\Omega_{\mathrm{hor}}(P,W)^{G}, which will be the subject of the next section. It contains some technical definitions that will be essential for the gauge theories. The reader can skip this paragraph and only return to it later when the physics demands these definitions.

Definition (Inner product on tensor space).

Let EE be a 𝕜\Bbbk-vector space with an inner product gg. This statement is just a technical generalisation of the well-known result for the case in which W=𝕜W=\Bbbk and P=MP=M. The proof can be found in [6].

Remark 1.3.11.

We have seen that we can construct a product connection when we are dealing with fibre bundles. Moreover, we know that P​BMPB_{M} has finite products. The question is whether the product of two principal connections is again a principal connection. Obviously, the answer is yes. [6] This connection is very important in gauge theory. Physicists often call it the spliced connection, in line with their interesting terminology for the product of two principal bundles.

1.3.3 Induced Connections

We have seen that, given a principal GG-bundle P⟶π~MP\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\tilde{\pi}}}{{\longrightarrow}}M and an action G×S⟶λSG\times S\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\lambda}}{{\longrightarrow}}S of GG on a manifold SS, we can construct an associated fibre bundle P⁡[λ]P[\lambda] with fibre SS. Suppose that PP is also equipped with a principal connection T​P⟶PV=ζ∘ωV​PTP\stackrel{{\scriptstyle P_{V}=\zeta\circ\omega}}{{\longrightarrow}}VP. The question is whether this induces a connection on the associated bundle in some natural way. This is indeed the case and the correspondence is particularly simple. It will be useful especially when we are dealing with the associated bundles that are part of an equivalence, as discussed in section 1.1.6. Before we construct the induced connection, however, let us stop for a moment to think about what precisely a connection on the associated bundle would have to be.

Remember that we defined the associated bundle P⁡[λ]P[\lambda] as the quotient P×S/GP\times S/G, where GG acts on P×SP\times S on the right by P×S×G⟶ρ×λ−1P×SP\times S\times G\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rho\times\lambda^{-1}}}{{\longrightarrow}}P\times S. By this notation I mean (p,s,g)↦(ρ⁡(p,g),λ⁡(g−1,s))(p,s,g)\mapsto(\rho(p,g),\lambda(g^{-1},s)). It is useful to describe tangent vectors to P⁡[λ]P[\lambda] by representatives: every tangent vector at [p,s][p,s] can be written as T​q​(ξp,ηs)Tq(\xi_{p},\eta_{s}) for some (ξp,ηs)∈Tp​P×Ts​S(\xi_{p},\eta_{s})\in T_{p}P\times T_{s}S.

PV​[λ]​(T​q​(ξp,ηs)):=T​q​(PV​(ξp),ηs).P_{V}[\lambda](Tq(\xi_{p},\eta_{s})):=Tq(P_{V}(\xi_{p}),\eta_{s}).

if we use the notation TcFT^{F}_{c} for the parallel transport along cc on a fibre bundle F⟶MF\stackrel{{\scriptstyle}}{{\longrightarrow}}M. This follows almost immediately from the uniqueness of solutions of ODEs. That is, after we observe that

1.3.4 Principal Connections Are Complete

Why are we interested in principal connections in the first place? One major advantage of such a connection is that it is automatically a complete connection: parallel transport is globally defined along any curve. One consequence is that we can construct a holonomy group.

Theorem 1.3.12.

Principal connections are complete, i.e. for every curve I⟶cMI\stackrel{{\scriptstyle c}}{{\longrightarrow}}M, the parallel transport is defined for all times: Pc⁡(0)×I⟶TcPP_{c(0)}\times I\stackrel{{\scriptstyle T_{c}}}{{\longrightarrow}}P.

Proof.

Let P⟶π~MP\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\tilde{\pi}}}{{\longrightarrow}}M be a principal GG-bundle that is equipped with a principal connection ω\omega and let I⟶cMI\stackrel{{\scriptstyle c}}{{\longrightarrow}}M be a C1C^{1}-curve. We want to show that parallel transport is defined globally, so, in the notation of theorem 1.2.9, Ωc=Pc⁡(0)×I\Omega_{c}=P_{c(0)}\times I.

The idea of the proof is that it is easy to find some lift of cc to PP, which we can transform into a horizontal lift by the action of appropriate group elements. One easily derives the differential equation these group elements have to satisfy. Finally, a maximal solution to this differential equation is obtained by extending a local solution using the group multiplication.

The precise argument is the following. Using local trivialisations, it is easy to construct a curve I⟶dPI\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{\longrightarrow}}P, such that π~∘d=c\tilde{\pi}\circ d=c and d⁡(0)=pd(0)=p, if p∈Pc⁡(0)p\in P_{c(0)}. We look for a smooth curve I⟶gGI\stackrel{{\scriptstyle g}}{{\longrightarrow}}G, such that chor​(t):=ρ⁡(dt,gt)c_{\mathrm{hor}}(t):=\rho(d_{t},g_{t}) is a horizontal lift of cc: π~∘chor=c\tilde{\pi}\circ c_{\mathrm{hor}}=c and chor′​(t)∈H​Pc_{\mathrm{hor}}^{\prime}(t)\in HP, for all t∈It\in I. (Here we write dtd_{t} for d⁡(t)d(t) and similarly for gtg_{t}.)

We verify what conditions the second demand imposes on t↦gtt\mapsto g_{t}. In terms of ω\omega it reads

0=!ω⁡(dd​t​ρ​(dt,gt)).0\stackrel{{\scriptstyle!}}{{=}}\omega\left(\frac{d}{dt}\rho(d_{t},g_{t})\right).

Now, by the Leibniz rule, dd​t​ρ​(dt,gt)=T​ρgt​d˙t+T​ρdt​g˙t\frac{d}{dt}\rho(d_{t},g_{t})=T\rho_{g_{t}}\dot{d}_{t}+T\rho^{d_{t}}\dot{g}_{t}, where, as before, ρh​(p):=ρ⁡(p,h)=:ρp​(h)\rho_{h}(p):=\rho(p,h)=:\rho^{p}(h). 1.3.5 The Ambrose-Singer Theorem

In the case of a principal connection, the interpretation of the curvature as infinitesimal holonomy that we already observed in claim 1.2.10 takes a particularly simple form. This result is the famous theorem by Ambrose and Singer. [18]

Theorem 1.3.13 (Ambrose-Singer).

Let P⟶π~MP\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\tilde{\pi}}}{{\longrightarrow}}M be a principal bundle with a principal connection ω\omega. Then its holonomy group at a point p0∈Pp_{0}\in P is a Lie group and its Lie algebra is isomorphic to the subalgebra of 𝔤\mathfrak{g} spanned by the elements of the form Ωpω​(X,Y)\Omega^{\omega}_{p}(X,Y), where pp runs over all points that can be connected to p0p_{0} by a horizontal curve and X,YX,Y run over all elements of Tp​PT_{p}P.

1.4 Connections on Vector Bundles

Just as in the case of principal bundles, where we singled out certain connections that are compatible with the group action, we have certain preferred connections on vector bundles: those that are compatible with the linear structure on each fibre. In fact, we will see that, in some sense, these are a special case of the principal connections we have already seen. What does this compatibility mean concretely?

Let V⟶πMV\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\pi}}{{\longrightarrow}}M be a vector bundle with a connection PVP_{V}. In section 1.2.1, we have defined T​V⟶PVV​V⊂T​VTV\stackrel{{\scriptstyle P_{V}}}{{\longrightarrow}}VV\subset TV to be a morphism of vector bundles over VV, since this was the only vector bundle structure that was at hand. Now, however, T​VTV also has a second vector bundle structure, namely T​V⟶T​πT​MTV\stackrel{{\scriptstyle T\pi}}{{\longrightarrow}}TM. We would like the vertical part of a tangent vector, after identifying V​V≅V×MVVV\cong V\times_{M}V, to respect the linear structure on the fibres of T​V⟶T​πT​MTV\stackrel{{\scriptstyle T\pi}}{{\longrightarrow}}TM as well. When this is the case, we call PVP_{V} an affine connection.

Note that, in the light of equation 1.2, the affinity of the connection is equivalent to the linearity over the ring C∞​(M)C^{\infty}(M) of the Christoffel forms in the second argument: Γα​(X,f⋅v)=f⋅Γα​(X,v)\Gamma^{\alpha}(X,f\cdot v)=f\cdot\Gamma^{\alpha}(X,v). This means that we can view X↦Γα​(X,−)X\mapsto\Gamma^{\alpha}(X,-) as an End⁡(𝕜k)\mathrm{End}(\Bbbk^{k})-valued 11-form Γα∈Ω1​(Uα,End⁡(𝕜k))\Gamma^{\alpha}\in\Omega^{1}(U_{\alpha},\mathrm{End}(\Bbbk^{k})).

This means that the equation that defines parallel transport will be a linear one, whose solution, obviously, depends on the initial values in a linear way. This means that the parallel transport along a curve cc over time tt defines a (fibrewise linear) map Vc⁡(0)⟶Tc​(−,t)Vc⁡(t)V_{c(0)}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle T_{c}(-,t)}}{{\longrightarrow}}V_{c(t)}. We will denote this map by Tc,tT_{c,t}. (Compare this with the GG-equivariance of the parallel transport on a GG-principal bundle with an equivariant connection.)

1.4.1 Covariant Derivatives

There is hardly any mathematical device that is more recurrent in the theory of general relativity than the so-called covariant derivative. It arises wherever an ordinary derivative would appear in non-relativistic physics. We will see that this derivative is closely related to the notions we discussed in the previous paragraphs: connections, curvature, horizontal lifts, Christoffel forms and parallel transport. It is defined as follows.

Let us take a vector field M⟶XT​MM\stackrel{{\scriptstyle X}}{{\longrightarrow}}TM and a section M⟶σVM\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\sigma}}{{\longrightarrow}}V. We can canonically identify V​Vv=Tv​Vπ⁡(v)≅Vπ⁡(v)VV_{v}=T_{v}V_{\pi(v)}\cong V_{\pi(v)} for every v∈Vv\in V. On the level of vector bundles over MM this becomes an isomorphism

This means that the effect of the connection PVP_{V} is entirely captured in the map K:=π2∘Φ−1∘PVK:=\pi_{2}\circ\Phi^{-1}\circ P_{V}, known as the connector of the connection. For an affine connection, KK is a map of vector bundles (i.e. respects the linear structure on the fibres) in the following two senses:

The first linearity follows from the fact that PVP_{V} is a vector-bundle projection over VV; the second is precisely the affinity condition.

The covariant derivative ∇Xσ​(m):=K∘T​σ∘X⁡(m)\nabla_{X}\sigma(m):=K\circ T\sigma\circ X(m) of σ\sigma along XX is then an element of Vπ⁡(σ⁡(m))=VmV_{\pi(\sigma(m))}=V_{m}. ∇Xσ\nabla_{X}\sigma is simply a section ∇Xσ∈Γ⁡(V)\nabla_{X}\sigma\in\Gamma(V). This means that ∇X\nabla_{X} is an operator Γ⁡(V)⟶∇XΓ⁡(V)\Gamma(V)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\nabla_{X}}}{{\longrightarrow}}\Gamma(V). In particular, we can iterate it, to obtain higher covariant derivatives. Moreover, it has the following properties.

Nevertheless, the resemblance is not a coincidence. As we will see, it is a consequence of the fact that an affine connection is induced from a principal connection on the frame bundle.

1.4.3 Equivalent Notions of a Connection

In section 1.1.6, we have seen that there is an equivalence of categories between G​L​(𝕜k)GL(\Bbbk^{k})-principal bundles and kk-dimensional vector bundles over a manifold MM, in the form of the associated vector bundle construction and the frame bundle construction. The question is whether one can, given a suitable connection on a vector bundle, construct one on the frame bundle and vice versa. The answer turns out to be affirmative.

Claim 1.4.6.

Suppose V⟶πMV\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\pi}}{{\longrightarrow}}M is a kk-dimensional vector bundle. Then, there is a canonical one-to-one correspondence between affine connections on VV and principal connections on the frame bundle Fλ​(V)F^{\lambda}(V), where one direction of the correspondence is precisely the induced connection (if we use the natural identification Fλ​(V)​[λ]≅VF^{\lambda}(V)[\lambda]\cong V).

T​q​(PV′​(f,w),−)=PV′​[λ]∘T​q​((f,w),−)=!T​q​(PV∘(f,w),−).Tq(P_{V}^{\prime}(f,w),-)=P_{V}^{\prime}[\lambda]\circ Tq((f,w),-)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle!}}{{=}}Tq(P_{V}\circ(f,w),-).

Remark 1.4.7.

Perhaps this result would be better placed in section 1.3.3, in a more general form. Certainly, if one were to formulate an appropriate notion of a ‘(G,λ)(G,\lambda)-connection’ in a fibre bundle with structure group (G,λ)(G,\lambda), one would expect that the same construction would work to establish a one-to-one correspondence between such connections on the (G,λ)(G,\lambda)-fibre bundle and principal connections on the corresponding generalised frame bundle. (I would opt to define such connections as ones whose vertical projections are maps of (T​G,T​λ)(TG,T\lambda)-fibre bundles over T​MTM). One could even go a step further and define a category of (G,λ)(G,\lambda)-fibre bundles with (G,λ)(G,\lambda)-connections, in which a natural definition of arrows would be maps of (G,λ)(G,\lambda)-fibre bundles such that the two connections involved would be related by pullback along such a fibre bundle, and try to extend the equivalence of categories of theorem 1.1.3 to one between such categories. However, such a result would probably have few applications and would be established purely for aesthetic purposes. Therefore, it is omitted.

We see that we can interpret the theory of vector bundles with affine connections as a special case of that of principal bundles with equivariant connections. In particular, we have the following.

Corollary 1.4.8.

Affine connections are complete.

Proof.

In the light of claim 1.4.6, this follows immediately from the fact that the induced parallel transport on the associated bundle is qq-related to that on the original principal bundle, which we already know to be defined along all curves by theorem 1.3.12.

Of course, we could also write out the differential equation defining parallel transport in local coordinates, which would be linear in the case of an affine connection. The global existence theorem for linear differential equations would do the rest. ∎

To complete the equivalence between affine connections on a vector bundle and equivariant connections on its frame bundle, we state the following result, due to Kolář et al. [19], relating the two derivatives. We have seen in remark 1.3.9 that for a principal GG-bundle P⟶π~MP\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\tilde{\pi}}}{{\longrightarrow}}M and a vector space WW with a linear GG-action λ\lambda we have an identification Ωhork​(P,W)G⟶≃ΨλΩk​(M,P⁡[λ])\Omega_{\mathrm{hor}}^{k}(P,W)^{G}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\Psi_{\lambda}}}{{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\simeq}}{{\longrightarrow}}}}\Omega^{k}(M,P[\lambda]). In particular, we can identify an equivariant function P⟶ΦWP\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\Phi}}{{\longrightarrow}}W with a section σ\sigma of the associated bundle P⁡[λ]P[\lambda]. In the presence of a connection, we can take the exterior covariant derivative along the horizontal lift of a vector field X∈𝒳⁡(M)X\in\mathcal{X}(M) on one side to obtain another equivariant function P⟶dω​Φ​(Xhor)WP\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d^{\omega}\Phi(X_{\mathrm{hor}})}}{{\longrightarrow}}W and on the other we can take the covariant derivative (of the induced connection) along the vector field to obtain another section: ∇Xσ∈Γ⁡(P⁡[λ])\nabla_{X}\sigma\in\Gamma(P[\lambda]). One wonders if the two are related. Indeed, they turn out to coincide in the identification Ψλ\Psi_{\lambda}.

If we extend ∇\nabla from Ω0​(M,P⁡[λ])=Γ⁡(P⁡[λ])\Omega^{0}(M,P[\lambda])=\Gamma(P[\lambda]) to Ωk​(M,P​[λ])\Omega^{k}(M,P[\lambda]), by setting, for α∈Ωk​(M,P⁡[λ])\alpha\in\Omega^{k}(M,P[\lambda]) and X0,…,Xk∈𝒳⁡(M)X_{0},\ldots,X_{k}\in\mathcal{X}(M):

(d∇​α)​(X0,…,Xk):=∑i=0k(−1)i​∇Xi(α⁡(X0,…,Xi^,…​Xk))(d_{\nabla}\alpha)(X_{0},\ldots,X_{k}):=\sum_{i=0}^{k}(-1)^{i}\nabla_{X_{i}}(\alpha(X_{0},\ldots,\hat{X_{i}},\ldots X_{k}))
+∑0≤i<j≤k(−1)i+jα([Xi,Xj],X0,…,X^i,…,X^j,…Xk)+\sum_{0\leq i<j\leq k}(-1)^{i+j}\alpha([X_{i},X_{j}],X_{0},\ldots,\hat{X}_{i},\ldots,\hat{X}_{j},\ldots X_{k})

- this is just the definition of the ordinary differential dd with ∇Xi\nabla_{X_{i}} replacing ℒXi\mathcal{L}_{X_{i}} - then we have the following.

Claim 1.4.9.

d∇d_{\nabla} acts on P⁡[λ]P[\lambda]-valued differential forms on MM as dωd^{\omega} does on equivariant horizontal ones on PP, in the sense that

The proof, which can be found in [19], proceeds as one would expect. One first checks the identity on Ω0\Omega^{0}. (This is a short computation.) Next, one extends it to elements of Ωk​(M,P​[λ])\Omega^{k}(M,P[\lambda]) that can be decomposed as σ⊗η\sigma\otimes\eta, with σ∈Ω0​(M,P⁡[λ])\sigma\in\Omega^{0}(M,P[\lambda]) and η∈Ωk​(M)\eta\in\Omega^{k}(M). 1.4.4 Categorical Constructions on Affine Connections

It turns out to be possible to transfer a connection to quite a few categorical constructions we can build out of a vector bundle. We can, for instance, give a sensible definition of a dual connection on the dual bundle of a vector bundle with a connection. The same applies for the tensor product.

Suppose V⟶πMV\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\pi}}{{\longrightarrow}}M is a 𝕜k\Bbbk^{k}-vector bundle that is equipped with an affine connection PVP_{V}. We have seen in claim 1.4.6 that this canonically induces a connection FT​λ​(PV)F^{T\lambda}(P_{V}) on the frame bundle Fλ​(V)F^{\lambda}(V). Note that we have a canonical left action λ∗\lambda^{*} of G​L​(𝕜k)GL(\Bbbk^{k}) on 𝕜k∗\Bbbk^{k}{}^{*} by (inverse) precomposition GL(𝕜k)∋g↦−∘g−1∈GL(𝕜k)∗GL(\Bbbk^{k})\ni g\mapsto-\circ g^{-1}\in GL(\Bbbk^{k}{}^{*}). We are in the familiar setting in which we construct an associated vector bundle. Note that this is just the dual vector bundle V∗⟶π∗MV^{*}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\pi^{*}}}{{\longrightarrow}}M. This gives us a canonical way to transfer the connection on VV to V∗V^{*}: FT​λ​(PV)F^{T\lambda}(P_{V}) induces an affine connection on the associated bundle V∗→MV^{*}\to M:  FT​λ​(PV)​[λ∗]F^{T\lambda}(P_{V})[\lambda^{*}]. It is easily verified, using the characterisation of the covariant derivative given in claim 1.4.3 in combination with the Leibniz rule, that this yields the following relation between the covariant derivatives:

⟨∇X∗ξ,σ⟩+⟨ξ,∇Xσ⟩=X⁡(⟨ξ,σ⟩),\langle\>\nabla^{*}_{X}\xi\,,\sigma\>\rangle+\langle\>\xi\,,\nabla_{X}\sigma\>\rangle=X(\langle\>\xi\,,\sigma\>\rangle),

where X∈𝒳⁡(M)X\in\mathcal{X}(M), σ∈Γ⁡(π)\sigma\in\Gamma(\pi) and ξ∈Γ⁡(π∗)\xi\in\Gamma(\pi^{*}).

In the case of a complex vector bundle, there is the concept of the complex conjugate bundle. This is easily seen to be an associated bundle as well. Indeed, let V⟶πMV\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\pi}}{{\longrightarrow}}M be a vector bundle and describe it as an associated bundle of P⟶π~MP\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\tilde{\pi}}}{{\longrightarrow}}M corresponding to the canonical action λ\lambda of G​L​(ℂk)GL(\mathbb{C}\;^{k}) on ℂk\mathbb{C}\;^{k}. Then we have an action λ¯\bar{\lambda} of G​L​(ℂk)GL(\mathbb{C}\;^{k}) on ℂk¯\overline{\mathbb{C}\;^{k}}, by λ¯​(g,v¯):=λ⁡(g,v)¯\bar{\lambda}(g,\bar{v}):=\overline{\lambda(g,v)}. This induces a connection on the complex conjugate bundle V¯⟶π¯M\bar{V}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\bar{\pi}}}{{\longrightarrow}}M. The covariant derivative ∇¯\bar{\nabla} of this complex conjugate connection acts on sections ψ∈Γ⁡(π¯)\psi\in\Gamma(\bar{\pi}) as one would expect:

∇¯X​ψ=∇Xψ¯¯,\bar{\nabla}_{X}\psi=\overline{\nabla_{X}\bar{\psi}},

where ∇\nabla is the covariant derivative of the original connection on π\pi (of which we understand ψ¯\bar{\psi} to be a section). This construction is important in physics when one encounters spinors.

Similarly, if V′⟶π′MV^{\prime}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\pi^{\prime}}}{{\longrightarrow}}M is a second vector bundle, of dimension, say, ll over 𝕜\Bbbk, on which an affine connection PV′P_{V}^{\prime} is defined, we have a canonical notion of a tensor product connection on V⊗V′⟶π⊗π′MV\otimes V^{\prime}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\pi\otimes\pi^{\prime}}}{{\longrightarrow}}M. Again, we note that we obtain principal connections FT​λ​(PV)F^{T\lambda}(P_{V}) and FT​λ′​(PV′)F^{T\lambda^{\prime}}(P_{V}^{\prime}) on the frame bundles. This defines a principal connection FT​λ​(PV)×MFT​λ′​(PV′)F^{T\lambda}(P_{V})\times_{M}F^{T\lambda^{\prime}}(P_{V}^{\prime}) on the spliced principal G​L​(𝕜k)×G​L​(𝕜l)GL(\Bbbk^{k})\times GL(\Bbbk^{l})-bundle Fλ​(V)×MFλ′​(V′)→MF^{\lambda}(V)\times_{M}F^{\lambda^{\prime}}(V^{\prime})\to M. Again, we can form an associated vector bundle by the tensor product action λ⊗λ′\lambda\otimes\lambda^{\prime} of G​L​(𝕜k)×G​L​(𝕜l)GL(\Bbbk^{k})\times GL(\Bbbk^{l}) on 𝕜k⊗𝕜l\Bbbk^{k}\otimes\Bbbk^{l}. This vector bundle is, of course, just the tensor product bundle V⊗V′→MV\otimes V^{\prime}\to M. Since we have realised this bundle as an associated bundle, we obtain an induced connection (FT​λ​(PV)×MFT​λ′​(PV′))​[λ⊗λ′](F^{T\lambda}(P_{V})\times_{M}F^{T\lambda^{\prime}}(P_{V}^{\prime}))[\lambda\otimes\lambda^{\prime}] on it. In terms of the covariant derivative, this means that,

∇X⊗(σ⊗σ′)=(∇Xσ)⊗σ′+σ⊗(∇X′σ′),{}^{\otimes}\nabla_{X}(\sigma\otimes\sigma^{\prime})=(\nabla_{X}\sigma)\otimes\sigma^{\prime}+\sigma\otimes(\nabla^{\prime}_{X}\sigma^{\prime}),

if X∈𝒳⁡(M)X\in\mathcal{X}(M), σ∈Γ⁡(π)\sigma\in\Gamma(\pi) and σ′∈Γ⁡(π′)\sigma^{\prime}\in\Gamma(\pi^{\prime}) and if we denote the covariant derivative on V⊗V′V\otimes V^{\prime} by ⊗∇{}^{\otimes}\nabla. Again, this identity is almost immediate if one uses the relation of claim 1.4.3 between the covariant derivative and parallel transport. Note that physicists use these induced connections all the time when dealing with tensor bundles, for example in the context of general relativity.

An analogous construction for which we can also define an induced connection is the direct sum (categorical product). We have already seen how to define the product connection for general fibre bundles. In this context, it will be no different. We can also understand the direct sum bundle to be an associated bundle and construct the connection as we did for the tensor product (using the direct sum action). The result on the covariant derivative is as follows:

∇X⊕(σ⊕σ′)=∇Xσ⊕∇X′σ′{}^{\oplus}\nabla_{X}(\sigma\oplus\sigma^{\prime})=\nabla_{X}\sigma\oplus\nabla^{\prime}_{X}\sigma^{\prime}

and we extend by linearity.

Finally, the construction works equally for Hom\mathrm{Hom}-bundles. Obviously, these can also be seen as associated vector bundles, since we have the canonical isomorphism Hom⁡(V,V′)≅V∗⊗V′\mathrm{Hom}(V,V^{\prime})\cong V^{*}\otimes V^{\prime}.

1.5 Manifolds with Connections

An important context in which one encounters connections is through a (pseudo-)metric on the tangent bundle of a manifold MM. This induces the so-called Levi-Civita connection on T​MTM. This subject, however, will be dealt with in section 1.6.

The more general class of arbitrary affine connections on a tangent bundle is dealt with first, in the hope that the reader realises which aspects are special to the case of Riemannian geometry and which structure derives from a more general principle. If a manifold is equipped with an affine connection on its tangent bundle, one sometimes simply says a connection is defined on the manifold. These manifolds form a broader class than the (pseudo)Riemannian manifolds. They have important applications.

For instance, they are used in the Newton-Cartan theory of gravity, which is a beautiful theory of Newtonian gravity, using a geometry very similar to that of the general theory of relativity. In this theory, the particle moves through Newtonian spacetime along geodesics that are determined by a non-metric connection. In this way, one can use the language of manifolds with connections to describe Newtonian as well as Einsteinian gravity and one can give a particularly clear demonstration that the latter reduces to the former in the limit c→∞c\to\infty. A useful reference on this subject is a text by Cartan himself, [8].

A first remark, although it is not of very fundamental importance, is the following. Let us adopt the notation T(k,l)​M:=⨂MkT​M⊗⨂lT∗​MT^{(k,l)}M:=\bigotimes_{M}^{k}TM\otimes\bigotimes^{l}T^{*}M. As we have seen, the affine connection on T​MTM induces one and therefore also a corresponding covariant derivative on these tensor bundles. We have seen that ∇Xσ​(m)\nabla_{X}\sigma(m) only depends on the value of XX at mm (and on the value of σ\sigma along a compatible curve). Therefore, if S∈Γ⁡(T(k,l)​M)S\in\Gamma(T^{(k,l)}M), then we can interpret ∇S\nabla S as an element of Γ⁡(T∗​M⊗T(k,l)​M)≅Γ⁡(T(k,l+1)​M)\Gamma(T^{*}M\otimes T^{(k,l)}M)\cong\Gamma(T^{(k,l+1)}M), where

(∇S)​(X,α1,…,αk,Y1,…,Yl)=(∇XS)​(α1,…,αk,Y1,…,Yl).(\nabla S)(X;\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{k},Y_{1},\ldots,Y_{l})=(\nabla_{X}S)(\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{k},Y_{1},\ldots,Y_{l}).

This is a notation that physicists use a lot in general relativity.

1.5.1 Geodesics

The most important new concept that we encounter when specialising from vector bundles with affine connections to manifolds with affine connections is that of geodesics. The reader might know the concept of a geodesic from Riemannian geometry, where a geodesic might be defined as a curve that locally minimises the path length (or, equivalently, the energy integral) between two points that lie on it. Of course, this definition cannot be formulated in the context of an arbitrary manifold with an affine connection. However, a geodesic can equivalently be defined as a curve whose tangent vectors are related by parallel transport along the curve itself. To be precise, a curve ]−ϵ,ϵ[⟶cM]-\epsilon,\epsilon[\stackrel{{\scriptstyle c}}{{\longrightarrow}}M is called a(n) (affinely parametrised) geodesic if

D​c′d​t=0.\frac{Dc^{\prime}}{dt}=0.

This definition makes equal sense when the connection is not a Levi-Civita connection of some metric.

Equivalently, for a given affine connection on T​MTM, one can define the geodesic spray to be the unique horizontal vector field WW on T​MTM such that T​π​(W⁡(v))=vT\pi(W(v))=v for all v∈T​Mv\in TM. A geodesic is then precisely the projection along π\pi of an integral curve of WW. More generally, we call a vector field WW on T​MTM a spray, if T​πM∘W=idT​MT\pi_{M}\circ W=\mathrm{id}_{TM} and, in a chart induced by the double tangent bundle functor, W⁡(x,y)=(x,y,y,Ax​(y))W(x,y)=(x,y;y,A_{x}(y)), where y↦Ax​(y)y\mapsto A_{x}(y) is quadratic. In this terminology, the geodesic spray of a connection is the unique horizontal spray.

1.5.2 Torsion

We have seen that an affine connection on the tangent bundle uniquely determines a geodesic spray. One can ask whether the converse is also true. The answer turns out to be: almost, once we fix a tensor field known as the torsion.

Given a manifold with an affine connection (M,PV)(M,P_{V}) we define the torsion T∈Γ⁡(T(1,2)​M)T\in\Gamma(T^{(1,2)}M) of the connection to be the (1,2)(1,2)-tensor

T⁡(X,Y):=∇XY−∇YX−[X,Y].T(X,Y):=\nabla_{X}Y-\nabla_{Y}X-[X,Y].

The following theorem gives an interpretation of the torsion tensor as the freedom in the choice of a connection, after we have specified a certain geodesic spray. [2]

Theorem 1.5.1 (Ambrose-Palais-Singer).

Let MM be a smooth manifold with a spray WW. Then, for each type (1,2)(1,2)-tensor field TT that is anti-symmetric in the last pair of arguments, there exists a unique affine connection on T​M⟶MTM\stackrel{{\scriptstyle}}{{\longrightarrow}}M such that WW is its geodesic spray and such that TT is its torsion.

In particular, for every affine connection on MM, we can find a unique torsion-free one that has the same geodesic spray. If we were to divide the affine connections on a manifold MM into equivalence classes of those that have the same geodesic spray, we could take this to be a canonical representative of each class. In computations, torsion-free connections are often easiest to work with; therefore, for example in the general theory of relativity, one uses this freedom to simplify calculations.

In light of this theorem, moreover, we see that it was no coincidence that Cartan was able to formulate Newtonian gravity using the geometry of an affine connection1919 19 Indeed, after adjoining the absolute time coordinate in Newton-Cartan spacetime, the Newtonian gravitational force of one point source gives rise to a spray whose spatial part is A(t,x)(t˙,x˙)=−γxt˙2/‖x‖3A_{(t,x)}(\dot{t},\dot{x})=-\gamma x\dot{t}^{2}/\left\lVert x\right\rVert^{3}, where γ\gamma is some scale constant for the gravitational interaction. Similarly, arbitrary Newtonian gravitational fields give spatial acceleration −∇Φ​(t,x)​t˙2-\nabla\Phi(t,x)\dot{t}^{2}. In particular, the acceleration is quadratic in the full spacetime velocity.. However, when Cartan formulated his Newton-Cartan theory in 1923, this result would not be proved for forty years.

Then, there is a canonical choice for a connection on MM (an affine connection on the tangent bundle). I will not give the standard derivation2020 20 This would involve demanding that the metric have covariant derivative zero and showing that this defines a unique connection for a specified torsion tensor (the canonical choice being torsion zero). My derivation is somewhat less standard, but yields the same connection. of this connection. The one I give might be somewhat more involved, but is more in line with the rest of this thesis. Chapter 2 Gauge Theories

This chapter will start with a very imprecise introduction, departing from Einstein’s general relativity and progressing along Maxwell’s electromagnetism towards a general first-quantised formalism of gauge theories (of the Yang-Mills kind). It will be assumed that the reader has some familiarity with the first two theories. I will therefore not be very strict when discussing them, leaving a lot of mathematical and physical details to be filled in by the reader. They only serve as a stepping stone, setting the philosophical tone for the culmination of this thesis in a general framework of gauge theories on principal bundles.

We will work in units c=GNewton=ℏ=ϵ0=μ0=1c=G_{\mathrm{Newton}}=\hbar=\epsilon_{0}=\mu_{0}=1.

2.1 Principal Bundles and Physics

After this abstract mathematical introduction, I can imagine the reader finds himself wondering how principal bundles ever found their way into physics. Funnily enough, the answer is to be sought in the abstract results of section 1.1, in particular the interpretation of principal bundles as bundles of frames and of their associated bundles. In this paragraph, I will try to sketch a philosophical framework of ideas, which I hope will help the reader understand the use of principal bundles in physics better. However, to fully appreciate the matter, a specific understanding of the technical details of the physical theories is essential.

The reader must realise that a conceptual shift has taken place in mathematical physics, over the last century, which is reflected in the mathematical language used to describe nature. I am talking, of course, about the transition from a coordinate approach to physics, using mostly tools from real analysis, towards a coordinate-free approach, focussing on the geometry of manifolds. I claim that this has at the same time been a shift in a philosophical point of view: from empiricist to realist.

In Newtonian mechanics, according to the principles of Galilean invariance, positions and velocities are defined only relatively. These quantities represent nothing intrinsic about what is happening in spacetime. They are the result of measurements that were performed by a certain observer and therefore tell us as much about this particular observer as they tell us about what that observer is observing. Here, the Galilean transformations relate one (inertial) observer to another and therefore capture, in a sense, the extent to which our description of nature is not intrinsic.

Of course, a similar principle remains when we proceed to the classical form of the special theory of relativity. Here, it is reflected by the Poincaré invariance11 1 The group of Poincaré transformations consists of all isometries of Minkowski spacetime, i.e. translations and Lorentz transformations. of the theory, the Poincaré transformations representing the relation between all possible (inertial) observers. If we include Maxwell’s electromagnetism, not only the positions and velocities are non-intrinsic quantities of spacetime: the same holds for electric and magnetic fields. What one observer would call an electric field would be a magnetic field for another observer. (See, for example, [16].)

With general relativity, however, the language of manifolds made its entrance in physics. By using this language, one seeks to remove this ambiguity in the description of nature. In general relativity, all quantities that are of physical interest are represented by mathematical objects related to the spacetime manifold MM that are independent of any choice of coordinates on MM or any choice of a (local) frame for T​MTM. Particular measurements of these quantities correspond to the description of these objects with respect to some coordinates or a (local) frame associated with the observer. One sees the same phenomenon in the recent Hamiltonian formulation of classical mechanics in the language of symplectic manifolds.

However, such an abstract framework is somewhat unnatural or, rather, somewhat incomplete. Since all measurements are made with respect to some reference frame (of an observer) and the measured quantity can never completely be divorced from the measurement process, it would seem foolish not to represent the measurement properly in the mathematical theory describing the physics. It is precisely here that principal bundles come into play. Principal bundles provide a more natural framework for modern theories of physics: they combine the realist aspect of an intrinsic description of nature and the empiricist aspect of the measuring process. They seem to be a useful compromise between the mathematician and the physicist.

In many theories of physics, observable quantities are represented by sections of certain fibre bundles over spacetime. If such a fibre bundle is well behaved, in the sense that its structure group is finite-dimensional (i.e. it is a (G,λ)(G,\lambda)-fibre bundle for an effective Lie group action λ\lambda), then we can (according to section 1.1.5) understand it to be an associated bundle of some principal bundle (the bundle of generalised frames). From this point of view the sections of the original fibre bundle can be interpreted (using claim 1.1.14) as equivariant maps from the principal bundle to some model fibre for the fibre bundle.

The reader is urged to think of the elements of the principal bundle as generalised frames for the original fibre bundle. This means that they correspond to different ways that we can convert the intrinsic dynamics that is described in an abstract way by a section of a fibre bundle to something concrete that we observe. These generalised frames are known to physicists as gauges, the structure group of the principal bundle is called the gauge group and an automorphism of the principal bundle that fixes the base is called a gauge transformation. In the case of a (metrised) vector bundle22 2 From a physical perspective, this is by far the most important case. this means that, by choosing a gauge, or an (orthonormal) frame for the fibre, we obtain a set of numbers: the coordinates of the section with respect to the frame.

The gauges often correspond to certain classes of observers (or, more precisely, to the clocks and metre sticks they use). Take, for example, Maxwell’s classical electromagnetism on flat spacetime. Here, the different inertial frames are precisely the gauges and the principal right action corresponds to the Lorentz transformations between the inertial frames. In general, however—in particular in modern particle physics—the gauges might represent something more abstract and might include the choice of a basis for the space of internal degrees of symmetry of a quantum particle (think of spin). The picture of the fibre of a principal bundle as a Lie group without a specified position of the identity then reflects the physical principle that all inertial observers are equivalent (and, more generally, that all gauges are equivalent). All equations of motion, as formulated on the principal bundle, are therefore invariant under the principal right action.

The general idea of the principal bundle approach is thus the simultaneous description of nature in a realist and empiricist fashion. The intrinsic description is made by viewing a quantity as a section of an associated bundle. Specific coordinate representations of this section are obtained by choosing a gauge and the structure group acts transitively and freely on the fibre, thereby interrelating all allowed gauges.

2.2 Einstein’s General Relativity

The idea of gauge theories starts with Einstein’s general theory of relativity, as this is where an intrinsic formulation in terms of manifold geometry was first introduced in physics. Remember that Einstein’s special theory of relativity is a theory of mechanics that was devised to solve the incompatibility between Newton’s laws of mechanics and Maxwell’s electromagnetism33 3 Indeed, analogues of Newton’s three laws of mechanics hold in special relativity.. Similarly, Einstein’s general theory of relativity was born from the need to make the special theory compatible with Newton’s law of gravitation44 4 Here, one can still formulate a form of Newton’s three laws of mechanics that holds equally in the presence of gravity.. It is a theory of gravity and mechanics; however, one would do it more justice by calling it a theory of spacetime geometry, as the paradigm shift it encompasses seems far more interesting than its precise numerical predictions. It is the best theory of gravity we have and its predictions, such as the perihelion shift of Mercury, gravitational lensing, gravitational redshift and even (arguably) the existence of black holes have been successfully verified. However, it is a classical theory in the sense that it does not deal with quantum-mechanical effects. The merger of quantum mechanics and general relativity is still, after almost a century, the holy grail of modern physics. I will briefly discuss the principles of general relativity from a point of view that fits in with the topics discussed in this thesis.

The central observation that might lead one to the mathematical framework of general relativity is the following. Let us consider a test particle in a gravitational field gg (a time-dependent vector field on ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3}) and let us denote its position at time tt by x⁡(t)∈ℝ3x(t)\in\mathbb{R}^{3}. Then Newton’s second law, combined with his law of gravitation, tells us that

mi​x′′​(t)=mg​g,m_{i}x^{\prime\prime}(t)=m_{g}g,

where mim_{i} is the particle’s ‘inertial mass’ and mgm_{g} is its ‘gravitational mass’, which we have known to coincide since Galileo; we therefore just talk about plain ‘mass’. This means that the equation of motion of the particle,

x′′​(t)=g,x^{\prime\prime}(t)=g,

does not depend on the particle’s mass. This principle is known as the weak equivalence principle. It opens the possibility to describe gravitation not as an interaction that might differ from particle to particle but as an intrinsic property of spacetime itself.

Another, more vague idea that motivates the formalism of general relativity is Mach’s principle. Briefly, it is the idea that the definition of what one would call non-accelerating or non-rotating motion should not be absolute. It should depend on all matter in the universe. Acceleration should be measured relatively. This principle is satisfied neither by Newtonian nor by special-relativistic mechanics.

These two principles combined with the requirement that general relativity reduces to special relativity and Newtonian gravity in the appropriate limits allegedly led Einstein to his theory of gravitation. [32] In general relativity, spacetime is represented by a four-dimensional pseudo-Riemannian manifold (M,g)(M,g) with metric signature (−1,+1,+1,+1)(-1,+1,+1,+1). There are, in general, no global notions of space and time. Of course, we obtain the Levi-Civita connection from the metric and therefore have a concept of spacetime geodesics, which will take the place of straight lines in special relativity, and of curvature. An observer is often modelled as a point particle and therefore as a curve ]−ϵ,ϵ[⟶γM]-\epsilon,\epsilon[\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\gamma}}{{\longrightarrow}}M. The fact that no observer can exceed the speed of light is formalised by the fact that γ\gamma has to be a timelike curve, i.e. its tangent vectors have a negative length.

Matter/energy is described by the so-called stress-energy tensor T∈Γ⁡(T∗​M⊗T∗​M)T\in\Gamma(T^{*}M\otimes T^{*}M), a symmetric (0,2)(0,2)-tensor on spacetime. The analogue of Newton’s second law, the so-called Einstein equation reads

8​π​T=Ric−12​𝒮​g=:G,8\pi T=\mathrm{Ric}-\frac{1}{2}\mathcal{S}g=:G,

where the Ricci tensor Ric∈Γ⁡(T∗​M⊗T∗​M)\mathrm{Ric}\in\Gamma(T^{*}M\otimes T^{*}M) is given by taking the trace55 5 What do we mean by the trace? By using the metric isomorphism T​M⟶gT∗​MTM\stackrel{{\scriptstyle g}}{{\longrightarrow}}T^{*}M we assume without loss of generality that TT is a tensor of type (0,n)(0,n). By taking the trace trk,l​T\mathrm{tr}^{k,l}\,T of TT over input kk and ll, we mean that we pick a local orthonormal frame (eμ)(e_{\mu}) for T​MTM and a dual frame (ωμ)(\omega^{\mu}) for T∗​MT^{*}M and set (trk,l​T)​(X1,…,X^k,…,X^l,…,Xn)=∑μ=03T⁡(X1,…,Xk−1,eμ,Xk+1,…,Xl−1,g−1​(ωμ),Xl+1,…,Xn)(\mathrm{tr}^{k,l}\,T)(X_{1},\ldots,\hat{X}_{k},\ldots,\hat{X}_{l},\ldots,X_{n})=\sum_{\mu=0}^{3}T(X_{1},\ldots,X_{k-1},e_{\mu},X_{k+1},\ldots,X_{l-1},g^{-1}(\omega^{\mu}),X_{l+1},\ldots,X_{n}) of the curvature tensor over the second and fourth inputs, so explicitly Ric⁡(X,Y)=(tr2,4​R)m​(X,Y)=tr⁡(Rm​(X,−)​Y)\mathrm{Ric}(X,Y)=(\mathrm{tr}^{2,4}\,R)_{m}(X,Y)=\mathrm{tr}\,(R_{m}(X,-)Y) (RR denotes the curvature tensor) and the curvature scalar 𝒮\mathcal{S} is defined to be 𝒮⁡(m):=tr​Ricm\mathcal{S}(m):=\mathrm{tr}\>\mathrm{Ric}_{m}. The right side of the Einstein equation is denoted by GG and is known as the Einstein tensor.

Just as Newton’s second law has to be completed with a specification of a form of the force FF (take, for example, the force of a spring that satisfies Hook’s law: F=−k​xF=-kx), Einstein’s equation has to be completed with a specification of the form of the stress-energy tensor, called an equation of state. There are many common forms that lead to relevant solutions: for instance, the stress-energy tensor of a perfect fluid66 6 This is used as a model for various states of matter ranging from dust clouds to the interior of stars. Moreover, it is used in the Robertson-Friedmann-Walker model of cosmology as the average energy-momentum tensor of our universe. [32] reads T=ρ​u⊗u+P⁡(g+u⊗u)T=\rho\,u\otimes u+P(g+u\otimes u), where ρ,P∈C∞​(M)\rho,P\in C^{\infty}(M) represent the mass density and the pressure, respectively, and u∈𝒳⁡(M)u\in\mathcal{X}(M) represents the unit tangent vectors to the world lines of the fluid particles. The expression for the stress-energy tensor of an electromagnetic field is also well-known and it can be found in section 2.3.

The Bianchi identity for the curvature RR of the Levi-Civita connection gives us the second important equation of general relativity:

tr1,2​(∇G)=0,\mathrm{tr}^{1,2}\,(\nabla G)=0,

where ∇\nabla denotes the covariant derivative of the connection on the (0,2)(0,2)-tensor bundle, induced by the Levi-Civita connection. The derivation of this result is a useful exercise for the reader, or can be found in any textbook on general relativity (take for instance [25]). The Einstein equation gives a physical interpretation of this equation as a generalised statement of energy-momentum conservation:

tr1,2​(∇T)=0.\mathrm{tr}^{1,2}\,(\nabla T)=0.

One of the best known statements of general relativity is that a point particle moves through spacetime along timelike geodesics. What is less known is that this is not an extra assumption but indeed a consequence of the previous equation, if one models a point particle as a limit of certain stress-energy tensors with decreasing support. This result is clearly explained in [11].77 7 In physics textbooks the result is usually derived arguing that on physical grounds an action principle should hold for the motion of the point particle, i.e. they argue that the energy integral of the point particles should be stationary. Of course, we have seen in section 1.6 that this is precisely saying that they should be geodesics of the Levi-Civita connection of the metric.

Although I have never found the comparison in the literature, it seems almost foolish not to make the following remark, in the context of this thesis. I encourage the reader to compare the Einstein equation with the (second) inhomogeneous Maxwell/Yang-Mills equation and to compare this equation of energy-momentum conservation with the (first) homogeneous Maxwell/Yang-Mills equation. Note that in all cases the inhomogeneous equation involves sources of the fields, while the homogeneous equation, which is actually a Bianchi identity in disguise, does not.

Finally, it is useful to formulate an action from which the Einstein equation follows.88 8 I will not be very formal about this, since I will be dealing with action principles in a formal way later on. However, this remark should help sketch the resemblance between Einstein’s general theory of relativity and more modern gauge theories we will see later. This was first done by Hilbert. The action he found was

S⁡(g):=∫M𝒮​μ,S(g):=\int_{M}\mathcal{S}\;\mu,

which is known as the Einstein-Hilbert action. Here μ\mu denotes the Lorentzian volume element on MM which we know to exist if MM is oriented. (If MM is non-orientable, the use of the orientation can be avoided, as we shall later see. Moreover, if MM is non-compact, the integral might not converge. Both of these issues are dealt with by considering the integral over small patches of MM and demanding it to be stationary on each patch.) If we see this action as a function from the infinite-dimensional manifold of Lorentzian metrics on MM to the real numbers, we find that the vacuum Einstein equation is satisfied by gg precisely if SS has a stationary point at gg. [32]

2.3 Maxwell’s Electromagnetism

This paragraph on electromagnetism will serve as a stepping stone for proceeding to general Yang-Mills theory. I will start by discussing Maxwell’s electromagnetism and will demonstrate that, in a natural fashion, this can give rise to considering a certain principal U⁡(1)U(1)-bundle over spacetime: we interpret electromagnetism as a Yang-Mills theory.

Let (M,g)(M,g) be a four-dimensional Lorentz manifold, representing spacetime. We will use the metric convention (−1,+1,+1,+1)(-1,+1,+1,+1). Classical electromagnetism is usually described by a 11-form j∈Ω1​(M)j\in\Omega^{1}(M), representing the electric charge and current, and a 22-form F∈Ω2​(M)F\in\Omega^{2}(M), representing the electromagnetic field strength. These charges and electromagnetic fields interact according to Maxwell’s equations, which, in modern language, take the form

d​F=0andδ​F=j,dF=0\quad\textnormal{and}\quad\delta F=j,

where we write δ\delta for the codifferential Ωk​(M)⟶δΩk−1\Omega^{k}(M)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\delta}}{{\longrightarrow}}\Omega^{k-1}, which is related to Ωk​(M)⟶dΩk+1\Omega^{k}(M)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{\longrightarrow}}\Omega^{k+1} by the Hodge star as follows. On a pseudo-Riemannian manifold (M,g)(M,g)

δ=sign(g)(−1)n​k+n+1∗d∗,\delta=\mathrm{sign}\;(g)(-1)^{nk+n+1}*d*,

where n=dimMn=\dim M and sign⁡(g)=±1\mathrm{sign}\;(g)=\pm 1 denotes the signature of the metric (so in our case n=4n=4 and sign⁡(g)=−1\mathrm{sign}\;(g)=-1).

These equations describe the propagation of electromagnetic fields along spacetime. Of course, if these electromagnetic fields carry a significant amount of energy, this influences the geometry of spacetime. The electromagnetic contribution to the stress-energy tensor is given by ([32])

T=14​π​(tr2,4​F⊗F−14​g⊗tr1,3​tr2,4​F⊗F).T=\frac{1}{4\pi}\left(\mathrm{tr}^{2,4}F\otimes F-\frac{1}{4}g\otimes\mathrm{tr}^{1,3}\mathrm{tr}^{2,4}F\otimes F\right).

This set of three equations forms the foundation of a theory of electromagnetism on curved spacetime, known as the Einstein-Maxwell formalism.

Of course, we can give physical interpretations to these differential forms. Suppose ]−ϵ,ϵ[⟶cM]-\epsilon,\epsilon[\stackrel{{\scriptstyle c}}{{\longrightarrow}}M is the world line of an observer, i.e. an affinely parametrised timelike geodesic (so g⁡(c′​(t),c′​(t))=−1g(c^{\prime}(t),c^{\prime}(t))=-1). This is called the observer’s proper time parametrisation. We can find a neighbourhood U⊂MU\subset M of c⁡(0)c(0) on which geodesic normal coordinates (xμ)0≤μ≤3(x^{\mu})_{0\leq\mu\leq 3} are defined such that x0​(c​(t))=tx^{0}(c(t))=t. The interpretation of these coordinates will be what the observer would call time and space, (xμ)1≤μ≤3(x^{\mu})_{1\leq\mu\leq 3} being the space coordinates and x0x^{0} the time. This chart defines a local frame for T​MTM and, more generally, for an arbitrary tensor bundle of MM. Let us write Tn​…​pk​…​mT^{k\ldots m}_{n\ldots p} for the component of a tensor TT with respect to the basis vector ∂∂xk⊗…⊗∂∂xm⊗d​xn⊗…⊗d​xp\frac{\partial}{\partial x^{k}}\otimes\ldots\otimes\frac{\partial}{\partial x^{m}}\otimes dx^{n}\otimes\ldots\otimes dx^{p}. Then the interpretations of jj and FF are the following for the observer.

j0j_{0} is interpreted as a −ρ-\rho, where ρ\rho is the electric charge density, while j1j_{1}, j2j_{2} and j3j_{3} correspond to the three spatial components of the electric current density. Moreover,

(Fμ​ν)0≤μ,ν≤3=(0E1E2E3−E10−B3B2−E2B30−B1−E3−B2B10),(F_{\mu\nu})_{0\leq\mu,\nu\leq 3}=\left(\begin{array}[]{cccc}0&E_{1}&E_{2}&E_{3}\\ -E_{1}&0&-B_{3}&B_{2}\\ -E_{2}&B_{3}&0&-B_{1}\\ -E_{3}&-B_{2}&B_{1}&0\end{array}\right),

where (E1,E2,E3)(E_{1},E_{2},E_{3}) and (B1,B2,B3)(B_{1},B_{2},B_{3}) are the spatial components of what the observer would call, respectively, electric and magnetic fields. It is easily verified that these equations give the ordinary Maxwell equations for EE and BB for Minkowski spacetime. [30]

The Maxwell equations tell us how a charge-current distribution jj creates an electromagnetic field. Conversely, the Lorentz force law describes how the electromagnetic field influences the motion of a charged point particle. In the context of general relativity it can be stated as follows. Let ]−ϵ,ϵ[⟶γM]-\epsilon,\epsilon[\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\gamma}}{{\longrightarrow}}M be the world line of a point particle with charge qq and mass mm and assume that it is parametrised such that g⁡(γ′​(t),γ′​(t))=−1g(\gamma^{\prime}(t),\gamma^{\prime}(t))=-1. Then, in any local frame (eμ)(e_{\mu}) for T​MTM, using the Einstein summation convention:

D​γ′d​t=qm​(iγ′​F)♯.\frac{D\gamma^{\prime}}{dt}=\frac{q}{m}\,\bigl(i_{\gamma^{\prime}}F\bigr)^{\sharp}.

(Here ♯\sharp denotes raising an index with the spacetime metric. Remember that D/d​tD/dt denotes the covariant derivative corresponding to the pullback connection γ∗​PV\gamma^{*}P_{V} if PVP_{V} denotes the Levi-Civita connection on T​MTM. Explicitly, for a vector field ss along γ\gamma, D​s/d​t=K∘s′Ds/dt=K\circ s^{\prime}.) In particular, a charged particle does not move along spacetime geodesics if electromagnetic fields are present!

It is important to note that the first Maxwell equation tells us that FF is closed. By the Poincaré lemma, this means that it is locally exact: for every point m∈Mm\in M, we find a neighbourhood U⊂MU\subset M and an A∈Ω1​(U)A\in\Omega^{1}(U) such that F=d​AF=dA on UU. This 11-form AA is known as the vector potential. It is worth noting that we can globally define AA in the case of Minkowski spacetime since it is star-shaped. Note that we have freedom in the choice of AA. Indeed, we can add arbitrary closed 11-forms to our vector potential. Of course, physicists use this to their advantage and choose appropriate local potentials for an enormous simplification of calculations.

Again, in the source-free case, we can find an action, called the Einstein-Hilbert-Maxwell action, from which the field equations will follow. Indeed, if locally F=d​AF=dA, then (g,A)(g,A) satisfies the Einstein equation with electromagnetic stress-energy and the source-free Maxwell equation precisely when

S⁡(g,A)=∫M(𝒮−12​tr1,3​tr2,4​(F⊗F))​μS(g,A)=\int_{M}(\mathcal{S}-\frac{1}{2}\mathrm{tr}^{1,3}\mathrm{tr}^{2,4}(F\otimes F))\mu

is stationary with respect to gg and to compactly supported variations of the potential AA.

2.4 Intermezzo: Geometrised Forces

There is an even more modern approach to classical electromagnetism, using the language of principal bundles, which this entire thesis has been working towards. Let us first ask why we are not satisfied with the formulation I just discussed. I think the primary argument, which I found in [6], might be the following: it does not provide enough geometric insight. Just like Einstein geometrised Newton’s theory of gravity, we would like to geometrise Maxwell’s electromagnetism.

In the absence of any forces, Newton’s second law tells us that the motion of a particle is a geodesic (i.e. straight line) in three-dimensional Euclidean space. This is a beautiful geometrical property of the theory: if the trajectories of two point particles are tangent at some point, they are the same (although they might be parametrised differently).

This simplicity is lost when we allow gravitational forces to act on the particles. Indeed, imagine we launch two projectiles from the same launching platform in exactly the same direction but with different velocity. It may happen that one escapes the earth’s gravitation while the other does not. This problem was resolved by Einstein. By considering a four-dimensional spacetime with a connection, we obtain new geodesics along which point particles travel. In this setting, the motion of two particles again coincides when it is tangent at some point of spacetime. The trajectories of the two projectiles were not tangent in Euclidean space but are in spacetime. By adding a dimension to our space, we geometrised the gravitational force.

However, the same problem still holds for electromagnetism. Suppose the two projectiles were charged, say electrons, then they would still follow different trajectories because of the earth’s magnetic field. We can hope to resolve this problem by a similar trick. We try to geometrise electromagnetism by considering the motion of the particle on a five-dimensional ‘charge-spacetime’ with a connection, on which the charged point particle will travel along geodesics. This construction was first worked out by Kaluza (1921) and Klein (1926).

2.5 Electromagnetism as a U⁡(1)U(1)-Gauge Theory

In modern language the Kaluza-Klein approach to electromagnetism is best described using a principal U⁡(1)U(1)-bundle P⟶π~MP\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\tilde{\pi}}}{{\longrightarrow}}M over spacetime. We will interpret the electromagnetic tensor as the curvature of some principal connection ω∈Ω1​(P,𝔲⁡(1))\omega\in\Omega^{1}(P,\mathfrak{u}(1)). The local choice of a gauge potential AαA_{\alpha} will then correspond to the pullback of the connection ω\omega along a local section eα∈Γ⁡(P|Uα)e_{\alpha}\in\Gamma(P|_{U_{\alpha}}) of π~\tilde{\pi}: Aα=i​e​eα∗​ωA_{\alpha}=ie\,e_{\alpha}^{*}\omega, where e∈ℝe\in\mathbb{R} is the fundamental unit of electric charge of which every other charge is a multiple99 9 Experiments tell us that such a smallest quantity of charge should exist. [24]. The question still is, however, what principal bundle we should be considering.

2.5.1 Potentials and Principal Connections

Suppose (Uα)(U_{\alpha}) is an open cover of MM and that we have made a choice of Aα∈Ω1​(Uα)A_{\alpha}\in\Omega^{1}(U_{\alpha}) of local electromagnetic vector potentials, i.e. d​Aα=F|UαdA_{\alpha}=F|_{U_{\alpha}}. ωβ=ωα−i​d​fα​β/e.\omega_{\beta}=\omega_{\alpha}-i\,df_{\alpha\beta}/e.

Let us write

gα​β:=exp(−ifα​β/e).g_{\alpha\beta}:=\exp(-if_{\alpha\beta}/e).

Then Uα∩Uβ⟶gα​βU⁡(1)U_{\alpha}\cap U_{\beta}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle g_{\alpha\beta}}}{{\longrightarrow}}U(1) and gα​β⋅gβ​γ⋅gγ​α=exp(−i(δf)α​β​γ/e)=1g_{\alpha\beta}\cdot g_{\beta\gamma}\cdot g_{\gamma\alpha}=\exp(-i(\delta f)_{\alpha\beta\gamma}/e)=1, where we write (δ​f)α​β​γ=fα​β+fβ​γ+fγ​α(\delta f)_{\alpha\beta\gamma}=f_{\alpha\beta}+f_{\beta\gamma}+f_{\gamma\alpha} (following the convention in Čech cohomology), if and only if (δ​f)α​β​γ∈!2​π​e​ℤ(\delta f)_{\alpha\beta\gamma}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle!}}{{\in}}2\pi e\mathbb{Z}. By theorem 1.1.1, we see that this is precisely the condition that states that (gα​β)(g_{\alpha\beta}) would define a coordinate principal U⁡(1)U(1)-bundle P⟶π~MP\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\tilde{\pi}}}{{\longrightarrow}}M, with local trivialisations which we shall write as (ψα)(\psi_{\alpha}). Now, why does this condition hold? (This is highly non-trivial.)

We easily see that d⁡((δ​f)α​β​γ)=d⁡(fα​β+fβ​γ+fγ​α)=Aβ−Aα+Aγ−Aβ+Aα−Aγ=0d((\delta f)_{\alpha\beta\gamma})=d(f_{\alpha\beta}+f_{\beta\gamma}+f_{\gamma\alpha})=A_{\beta}-A_{\alpha}+A_{\gamma}-A_{\beta}+A_{\alpha}-A_{\gamma}=0, thus (δ​f)α​β​γ(\delta f)_{\alpha\beta\gamma} is constant, i.e. equal to some cα​β​γ∈ℝc_{\alpha\beta\gamma}\in\mathbb{R}. Although it is far from easy to see that cα​β​γ∈2​π​e​ℤc_{\alpha\beta\gamma}\in 2\pi e\mathbb{Z}, this can indeed be argued on physical grounds1010 10 The argument rests on the fact that there is a smallest quantity of electric charge in nature..
